---
title: "Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression"
---

## Introduction {#sec-mlumr-intro}

Every method in this book until now has needed a bridge. The anchored indirect comparison of Chapter 14
subtracts two relative effects that share a common comparator $C$, and is exact only when the
$C$-anchored contrasts are transitive (@thm-bucher-unbiased); Chapter 16 showed that an effect modifier
distributed differently across the two trials breaks transitivity and that no manipulation of aggregate
data can repair it (@thm-failure-of-bucher). Population adjustment in Part IV rebuilt one trial's
population in the image of the other, but matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC, Chapter 18) and
simulated treatment comparison (STC, Chapter 19) still reported their answer in the *comparator*
population and, in their anchored form, still leaned on the shared comparator arm. Chapters 20 to 25 then
built multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR), which fits one individual-level model across a
*connected* network of individual patient data (IPD) and aggregate data (AgD) studies, integrates it over
any covariate distribution, and so reports a contrast in *any* target population (@thm-target-population-integral).
The connectivity was the last bridge standing: ML-NMR still required a path of shared treatments linking
every study to every other.

This chapter removes that bridge. The setting is the **unanchored disconnected network**: individual
patient data on one treatment, say the index treatment $A$, aggregate data on a comparator $B$, and *no
common comparator arm at all*. The two studies are single-arm trials, or arms extracted from larger
trials, that share no treatment. Such evidence is the daily reality of health-technology assessment (HTA)
for single-arm oncology trials, rare-disease registries, and real-world cohorts, where a randomized
head-to-head comparison does not exist and a connecting study cannot be found. Bucher cannot start, because
there is nothing to anchor on. Standard network meta-analysis cannot start, because the network is
disconnected. Unanchored MAIC and unanchored STC can produce a pairwise number, but only in the comparator
population and only under the strong conditional constancy of *absolute* effects (@thm-unanchored-maic-consistency,
@thm-stc-consistency). What this chapter develops, following @chandler2025mlumr, is the multilevel
generalization of that pairwise idea: **multilevel unanchored meta-regression** (ML-UMR), which carries the
integration machinery of ML-NMR, the Sobol' quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) rule and the Gaussian copula of
Chapter 22, into the unanchored setting and so reports the unanchored contrast in any target population
through one joint Bayesian likelihood.

The price of removing the anchor is a stronger identifying assumption, and naming it precisely is the
central conceptual work of the chapter. An anchored comparison needs only that relative effects transport:
study baselines and prognostic effects cancel against the common comparator, and effect modification is
allowed provided it is *shared* by the active treatments, the shared-effect-modifier assumption (SEMA,
@def-sema) that powers ML-NMR. An unanchored comparison has nothing to cancel against, so the arm surfaces
themselves must transport (conditional constancy of absolute effects, @def-conditional-constancy-absolute),
and the comparator surface, observed only as an aggregate, must be tied to the index surface. ML-UMR ties
them by the **shared prognostic factor assumption** (SPFA): the covariate-outcome slopes coincide,
$\boldsymbol\beta_A=\boldsymbol\beta_B$, so the $A$-versus-$B$ contrast has no effect modification. As a
slope restriction SPFA is SEMA applied to the pair $\{A,B\}$; what makes the unanchored comparison strictly
more demanding is the absolute constancy it must be combined with (@prp-spfa-vs-sema). SPFA is also
untestable when the comparator reports a single outcome summary. The
chapter is honest about this throughout: ML-UMR extends the *menu of target populations* available for an
unanchored comparison, at the cost of an assumption that the data cannot check.

The development proceeds in catalogue order. We fix the disconnected setting and its estimand
(@def-unanchored-network), isolate the structural fact that a single-arm study cannot separate its
baseline from its treatment effect, and state SPFA and its meaning (@def-spfa). We then build the
SPFA-invoking model and prove its identifiability from one IPD arm and one AgD arm (@thm-mlumr-model),
relax SPFA when the comparator reports subgroup outcomes (@thm-spfa-relaxation), and specialize the
aggregate integration to the unit hypercube (@thm-mlumr-qmc-marginalization). The survival case occupies
the center of the chapter: the proportional-hazards and accelerated-failure-time models, the integrated
censored likelihood, and the target-population survival, hazard, and restricted mean survival time
(@thm-mlumr-tte, @thm-mlumr-target-survival), with the reconstruction of pseudo-individual data from a
published Kaplan-Meier curve made precise (@thm-pseudo-ipd-reconstruction). The joint individual-plus-
aggregate likelihood (@thm-mlumr-joint-likelihood) ties the two data types into one posterior. We then
locate ML-UMR relative to its pairwise ancestor: it reduces to unanchored STC in the comparator population
and extends it elsewhere under SPFA (@thm-mlumr-stc-equivalence), and we compare SPFA with SEMA
(@prp-spfa-vs-sema). The chapter closes with the identifiability frontier and the inherent limits of
unanchored comparison (@thm-mlumr-identifiability), a fully worked binary example whose every number can be
checked by hand, a compact survival illustration, notes, and exercises. This chapter corresponds to results
M.1 to M.12 of the proof catalogue.

Throughout, $g$ is the link function (@def-link-function) on whose scale the linear predictor is built,
$A$ denotes the index treatment for which IPD are available, and $B$ denotes the comparator for which only
AgD are available. A population $\mathcal{P}$ is a distribution over the covariate space $\mathcal{X}$ with
density $f_{\mathcal{P}}$; the index trial's population is $\mathcal{P}_A$ with density $f_A$ and the
comparator's is $\mathcal{P}_B$ with density $f_B$, and a general reporting target is $\mathcal{P}^{*}$
with density $f_{*}$ and mean $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{*}$. We write $\boldsymbol\xi$ for the full parameter
vector and use the relative-effect and aggregation notation of [Notation](/notation.qmd) and of
Chapters 20 and 23.

## A concrete scenario and a plain-language roadmap {#sec-mlumr-roadmap}

Before any formalism, here is the clinical situation the chapter solves and the four-step logic that
solves it. We return to this scenario at every transition, and the fully worked arithmetic appears in
@sec-mlumr-example.

::: {#exm-mlumr-running}
## A single-arm oncology comparison (running example)
A sponsor seeks reimbursement for a new therapy $A$ in advanced melanoma. The evidence is asymmetric:

- **Index source (IPD on $A$).** A single-arm trial of $A$ with individual patient data: for each patient a
covariate vector (for example age, prior lines of therapy, and a binary biomarker such as PD-L1 status)
and an outcome (tumor response, yes or no; or a survival time).
- **Comparator source (AgD on $B$).** For standard chemotherapy $B$ there are no patient rows, only a
published report: the sample size, a table of baseline covariate means (and sometimes standard deviations
and a correlation matrix), and an outcome summary, either a response rate or a Kaplan-Meier survival curve.
- **No shared arm.** The trial of $A$ never gave $B$, and the report on $B$ never gave $A$; there is no
common comparator to anchor on. The network is *disconnected*.
- **The HTA question.** The reimbursement agency wants the effect of $A$ versus $B$ in a *decision
population* $\mathcal{P}^{*}$, whose covariate profile may match neither trial.

In the arithmetic of @sec-mlumr-example we make this numerical: one binary biomarker, an index fit giving
intercept $\alpha_A=-0.5$ and prognostic slope $\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}=1.0$ on the logit scale, and a
comparator report of $77$ responders out of $200$ with biomarker prevalence $0.5$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**The data flow in words.** ML-UMR answers the HTA question in four steps, each of which becomes a theorem
below. Read this once now; the rest of the chapter simply makes each step precise.

1. **Fit the index arm from its IPD.** Regress the index outcome on the covariates to estimate one
prognostic slope $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ (how strongly the covariates move the outcome) and one
index level $\alpha_A$ (the fitted outcome of arm $A$ at covariate zero). This is an ordinary
generalized-linear-model fit using only the index data (@thm-mlumr-model).
2. **Borrow the slope: the shared prognostic factor assumption.** Assume arm $B$ has the *same* covariate
slope as arm $A$ (@def-spfa). This is the price of having no anchor, and, as the chapter stresses
repeatedly, the two-study data cannot check it.
3. **Locate the comparator level from its AgD.** Use the single comparator outcome summary to pin the one
remaining unknown, the comparator level $\alpha_B$: choose $\alpha_B$ so that arm $B$'s model-predicted
average outcome, taken over the comparator's covariate distribution, equals the reported comparator outcome
(@thm-mlumr-model).
4. **Integrate over any target and contrast.** With both arm surfaces now known, average each arm's outcome
over any chosen target population $\mathcal{P}^{*}$ and contrast on the link scale (@eq-mlumr-estimand,
@thm-mlumr-target-survival).

The advertised advantage over the simpler pairwise methods is step 4: the freedom to choose
$\mathcal{P}^{*}$. The entire cost sits in step 2. Everything below unpacks these four steps and accounts
carefully for what each assumes. @tbl-mlumr-methods places ML-UMR beside the methods it generalizes; the
one column that separates them is "reports contrast in," and the price of the wider reach is the
assumption column.

| Method | Connected network? | Reports contrast in | Key assumption | What the data cannot check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bucher / anchored NMA | required | any population, via the common comparator | transitivity; balanced effect modifiers | checkable when a closed loop exists |
| Unanchored MAIC | not required | comparator population only | constancy of absolute effects | the transported absolute level |
| Unanchored STC | not required | comparator population only | constancy of absolute effects | the transported absolute level |
| ML-NMR | required (connected) | any target population | constancy of relative effects; SEMA where the network cannot estimate every interaction | the constancy assumption |
| ML-UMR | not required | any target population | constancy of absolute effects plus SPFA | the transported absolute level and the borrowed slope (Type 1) |

: Where ML-UMR sits among indirect-comparison methods. Anchored methods report in any population but need a
connected network; unanchored MAIC and STC drop the network but report only in the comparator population;
ML-UMR keeps the target-population freedom of ML-NMR without a network, paying with absolute constancy plus
SPFA.
{#tbl-mlumr-methods}

A reader who wants only the practical map may read @exm-mlumr-running, @tbl-mlumr-methods, and the worked
@sec-mlumr-example, then return to the theorems. The proofs are where the identifiability and equivalence
claims summarized here are earned.

## The unanchored disconnected network {#sec-mlumr-setting}

We fix the data structures and the estimand, and expose the structural obstruction that distinguishes the
unanchored case from everything before it.

::: {#def-unanchored-network}
## The unanchored disconnected two-study network
An **unanchored disconnected network** consists of two single-treatment data sources with no shared
treatment:

1. an **index source** providing individual patient data on treatment $A$: for each of $n_A$ patients a
covariate vector $\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and an outcome $y_i$, drawn from a
population $\mathcal{P}_A$ with covariate density $f_A$;

2. a **comparator source** providing aggregate data on treatment $B$: a sample size $n_B$, the marginal
covariate means $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_B=(\bar x_{B,1},\dots,\bar x_{B,d})$ (and, where reported, marginal
standard deviations and a covariate correlation matrix $\boldsymbol\Omega_B$), and an outcome summary, for
example an event count $r_B$ for a binary outcome, a sample mean $\bar y_B$ for a continuous outcome, or a
reconstructed Kaplan-Meier curve for a time-to-event outcome, from a population $\mathcal{P}_B$ with
covariate density $f_B$.

The treatments $A$ and $B$ share no common comparator arm; the network graph of Chapter 15 is
**disconnected**. The **estimand** is the marginal relative effect of $A$ versus $B$ in a stated target
population $\mathcal{P}^{*}$, on the link scale $g$,
$$
\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}^{*})\;:=\;g\!\big(\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}^{*})\big)-g\!\big(\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}^{*})\big),
\qquad
\bar\theta_k(\mathcal{P}^{*})=\int_{\mathcal{X}}g^{-1}\!\big(\eta_k(\mathbf{x})\big)\,f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
$$ {#eq-mlumr-estimand}
where $\eta_k(\mathbf{x})$ is the arm-$k$ linear predictor and $\bar\theta_k(\mathcal{P}^{*})$ is the
arm-$k$ marginal mean outcome in $\mathcal{P}^{*}$. In the notation of [Notation](/notation.qmd) this is the
target-population marginal contrast of @def-mlnmr-target-contrast, written here with $A$ as the subject so
that a positive $\Delta_{AB}$ favors the index treatment. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Reader translation.** Read @eq-mlumr-estimand from the inside out. For each arm,
$g^{-1}(\eta_k(\mathbf{x}))$ is that arm's predicted outcome on the natural scale (a response probability
for a binary outcome) at covariate value $\mathbf{x}$; integrating against $f_{*}$ *averages* this predicted
outcome over the target population, giving the arm's marginal mean $\bar\theta_k(\mathcal{P}^{*})$; finally
$g$ (the logit, say) is applied to each average, and the two are subtracted. In one sentence: average each
arm's outcome over the target population first, then contrast on the link scale. The order is deliberate.
Taking the link of the average, rather than the average of the conditional link-scale effect, is exactly
what makes the *marginal* estimand differ from the *conditional* one; that gap is non-collapsibility
(@def-non-collapsibility), and the worked @sec-mlumr-example displays it in two numbers you can check by
hand. A novice reader may find it helpful to picture $\mathcal{P}^{*}$ as a spreadsheet of covariate rows:
fill in each arm's predicted probability row by row, average the two columns, then compare the two averages
on the logit scale.

The estimand @eq-mlumr-estimand is identical in form to the ML-NMR target estimand of Chapter 23
(@eq-mlnmr-est-marg); what changes is the evidence available to identify the two arm linear predictors.
The defining difficulty of the unanchored case is recorded next.

::: {#lem-mlumr-single-arm-conflation}
## A single-arm study conflates baseline and treatment effect
Adopt the ML-NMR linear predictor of @def-individual-model, in which the arm-$k$ linear predictor in study
$j$ is $\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})=\mu_j+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_k+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$,
with $\mu_j$ the study baseline and $\gamma_k$ the treatment main effect. If a study contains a single arm
$k$, then the study baseline $\mu_j$ and the treatment main effect $\gamma_k$ enter the likelihood only
through their sum $\alpha:=\mu_j+\gamma_k$, and are not separately identified: any pair $(\mu_j,\gamma_k)$
and $(\mu_j+c,\gamma_k-c)$ with $c\in\mathbb{R}$ induces the same distribution of the data.
:::

::: {.proof}
With a single arm $k$ present in the study, every observation in the study has linear predictor
$\eta(\mathbf{x})=\mu_j+\gamma_k+\mathbf{x}^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k})$. The map
$(\mu_j,\gamma_k)\mapsto\eta(\cdot)$ depends on $(\mu_j,\gamma_k)$ only through the sum $\mu_j+\gamma_k$:
replacing $(\mu_j,\gamma_k)$ by $(\mu_j+c,\gamma_k-c)$ leaves $\mu_j+\gamma_k$, hence $\eta(\mathbf{x})$
for every $\mathbf{x}$, hence the conditional outcome law $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(\cdot\mid g^{-1}(\eta(\mathbf{x})))$,
hence the likelihood, unchanged. The parameter $c$ is therefore free, so $(\mu_j,\gamma_k)$ is not
identified; only the linear combination $\alpha=\mu_j+\gamma_k$ is. $\square$
:::

**Reader translation: what "identified" means, and why one arm cannot split the two pieces.** To say a
parameter is *identified* is to say the data pin it to a single value, even in the ideal limit of infinite
sample size; an *unidentified* parameter is one the data leave genuinely undetermined, so that no
estimator, however clever, can recover it. (This is the same notion introduced for regression in Part I;
we lean on it heavily below, so keep the one-line meaning in mind.) The content of
@lem-mlumr-single-arm-conflation is clinical, not just algebraic: from a single-arm trial you never observe
the enrolled patients *without* the treatment, so you cannot tell how much of the observed outcome level is
the treatment doing something ($\gamma_k$) and how much is merely the baseline prognosis of the patients
who happened to enroll ($\mu_j$). Only their sum, the arm's absolute outcome level $\alpha=\mu_j+\gamma_k$,
is visible; we call this sum the **conflated intercept** of the arm, and use the term freely below. An
anchored two-arm study escapes the trap because both arms share the one study baseline $\mu_j$, so
differencing the arms cancels $\mu_j$ and exposes $\gamma_k$; the unanchored design has no second arm to
difference against.

This rank deficiency is the algebraic heart of "unanchored." In a connected network the same treatment
appears in at least two studies, and the across-study comparison of arms that share a treatment removes the
baseline, leaving $\gamma_k$ identified; this is exactly what the anchor provides. With no shared
treatment there is no such comparison, and each single-arm source identifies only the *absolute* level of
its own arm, the conflated intercept $\alpha$. We therefore write the two arm linear predictors with
arm-specific intercepts and arm-specific covariate slopes,
$$
\eta_A(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_A+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_A,
\qquad
\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_B,
$$ {#eq-mlumr-two-arm}
where $\alpha_A=\mu_{\text{index}}+\gamma_A$ and $\alpha_B=\mu_{\text{comp}}+\gamma_B$ each conflate a
study baseline with a treatment main effect by @lem-mlumr-single-arm-conflation, and
$\boldsymbol\beta_k=\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ is the total covariate slope on arm $k$ in
the decomposition of @def-individual-model. (Recall from @def-individual-model, restated here because it is
the pivot of the whole chapter: $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ is the *prognostic* slope, the covariate effect shared
by every arm, the part of the outcome-covariate relationship that has nothing to do with treatment; and
$\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ is the arm-$k$ *effect-modification* slope, the treatment-by-covariate interaction
that bends one arm's covariate response relative to another. Their sum $\boldsymbol\beta_k=
\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ is the total slope that arm $k$'s own data actually trace out.
Prognostic means "predicts outcome regardless of treatment"; effect-modifying means "changes the treatment
contrast." Keep both meanings in view; SPFA is a statement about the second one.) The whole identification
problem is now visible: the IPD
identify $(\alpha_A,\boldsymbol\beta_A)$, but the AgD supply only a covariate distribution and one or a few
outcome summaries, far too little to identify the $(d+1)$-dimensional $(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)$.
Something must connect the two arms.

::: {.remark}
**Why this is a transportability problem.** Comparing $A$ and $B$ requires evaluating both arms in one
population. The arm-$A$ surface $\mu_A(\mathbf{x})=g^{-1}(\eta_A(\mathbf{x}))$ is estimated where $A$ was
observed, namely $\mathcal{P}_A$; to place it against $B$ in $\mathcal{P}_B$ or in any $\mathcal{P}^{*}$ we
must assume that the *same* conditional surface governs $\mathcal{P}_B$ and $\mathcal{P}^{*}$, an instance
of conditional transportability (@thm-conditional-transportability) and of the absolute-effect constancy
of @def-conditional-constancy-absolute. The general theory of Chapter 17 already told us the unanchored
price: @thm-unanchored-paic-consistency requires constancy of absolute effects and balance of every
imbalanced *prognostic* variable, not merely every effect modifier. Absolute constancy transports each arm's
surface across populations; SPFA, stated next, is the separate cross-treatment assumption that supplies the
comparator surface's slope, which one aggregate summary cannot identify. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This setup corresponds to M.1 in the proof catalogue.

## The shared prognostic factor assumption {#sec-mlumr-spfa}

We now state the assumption that connects the two arms and makes the unanchored comparison identifiable.

::: {#def-spfa}
## Shared prognostic factor assumption (SPFA)
In the two-arm unanchored model @eq-mlumr-two-arm, the **shared prognostic factor assumption** is the
hypothesis that the covariate-outcome slopes coincide across the two treatments,
$$
\boldsymbol\beta_A=\boldsymbol\beta_B=:\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}.
$$ {#eq-spfa}
The common value $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ is the single shared prognostic slope; the subscript PF
abbreviates *prognostic factor*. Equivalently, in the decomposition
$\boldsymbol\beta_k=\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ of
@def-individual-model, SPFA states that the effect-modification vectors are equal,
$\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}$, the slope restriction of SEMA (@def-sema). With no third
treatment in the network, take $A$ as the reference, $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\mathbf{0}$; SPFA then says
$\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}=\mathbf{0}$: **no effect modification of the $A$-versus-$B$ contrast**
(@def-effect-modifier). Under SPFA the two arm linear predictors are
$$
\eta_A(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_A+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}},
\qquad
\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}},
$$ {#eq-spfa-predictors}
differing only in the conflated intercepts $\alpha_A,\alpha_B$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**SPFA in plain language (the one assumption that pays for everything).** SPFA encodes a specific clinical
belief: *the way the covariates shape a patient's outcome is the same whichever of the two treatments the
patient receives.* Put the other way, the treatment does not act more strongly in one covariate subgroup
than another; there is no effect modification. A *plausible* case: two cytotoxic chemotherapies whose
benefit is roughly uniform across age and performance status, so older and younger patients gain similarly.
An *implausible* case: a targeted agent that works only in biomarker-positive patients, set against a
chemotherapy that works regardless of biomarker; here the treatment contrast depends sharply on the
biomarker, SPFA is false, and forcing it will bias any transported estimate. Two facts make SPFA the
delicate point of the method. First, it comes with absolute constancy: as a slope restriction SPFA is SEMA
for the pair $\{A,B\}$, but an anchored design applies SEMA to within-study contrasts against a common
comparator, in which study baselines and prognostic effects cancel, whereas ML-UMR must carry the arm
surfaces themselves across populations (@prp-spfa-vs-sema). Second, in the Type 1 setting (one comparator outcome summary) it
is *untestable*: the data are equally consistent with SPFA and with an effect-modifying alternative
(@thm-mlumr-identifiability), so SPFA must be argued from external clinical knowledge, not checked against
the two studies. @tbl-spfa-sema lays the two assumptions side by side. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

| Aspect | SEMA (anchored, ML-NMR) | SPFA (unanchored, ML-UMR) |
|---|---|---|
| Formal statement | $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}$ (interactions relative to $C$) | $\boldsymbol\beta_A=\boldsymbol\beta_B$ (total slopes) |
| In words | $A$ and $B$ are modified identically relative to $C$ | the covariates shape the outcome identically under $A$ and $B$ |
| $A$-versus-$B$ contrast | flat in $\mathbf{x}$ | flat in $\mathbf{x}$ |
| Constancy it is paired with | conditional constancy of *relative* effects | conditional constancy of *absolute* effects |
| Design it fits | connected, anchored network | disconnected, unanchored network |
| Testable from the data? | only with more than one study informing $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}$ (@prp-testable-untestable-constancy) | only with subgroup AgD (@thm-mlumr-identifiability) |
| Method it powers | ML-NMR | ML-UMR |

: SEMA versus SPFA. Both make the $A$-versus-$B$ contrast flat in the covariates. They differ in the
constancy assumption they are paired with: relative for the anchored design, absolute for the unanchored
one (@prp-spfa-vs-sema). {#tbl-spfa-sema}

The single line that SPFA buys is the following: it makes the conditional contrast a constant, which is
what lets the index IPD project the comparator arm everywhere.

::: {#lem-spfa-absolute-constancy}
## SPFA makes the conditional contrast constant
Under SPFA @eq-spfa, the conditional contrast of $A$ versus $B$ on the link scale is free of the covariate,
$$
\eta_A(\mathbf{x})-\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_A-\alpha_B
\qquad\text{for every }\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X},
$$ {#eq-spfa-constant-contrast}
and the arm-$B$ conditional surface is determined by the arm-$A$ surface and a single scalar level shift,
$$
\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=\eta_A(\mathbf{x})-(\alpha_A-\alpha_B).
$$ {#eq-spfa-projection}
Consequently, once $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ is known from the index IPD, knowledge of one scalar,
$\alpha_B$, determines $\eta_B(\mathbf{x})$, and hence $g^{-1}(\eta_B(\mathbf{x}))$, at *every* covariate
value, including values the comparator source never reported individually. SPFA links the two arms'
surfaces; it does not transport them across populations, which is conditional constancy of absolute
effects (@def-conditional-constancy-absolute).
:::

::: {.proof}
Subtract the two predictors of @eq-spfa-predictors:
$\eta_A(\mathbf{x})-\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=(\alpha_A+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})-
(\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})=\alpha_A-\alpha_B$, since the covariate terms are
identical and cancel; this is @eq-spfa-constant-contrast, free of $\mathbf{x}$. Rearranging gives
@eq-spfa-projection. The arm-$A$ surface $\eta_A(\cdot)=\alpha_A+(\cdot)^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$
is identified from the index IPD (a generalized linear model with full-rank design, @thm-mlumr-model below),
so $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ is known; @eq-spfa-projection then expresses $\eta_B$ in terms of the
known $\eta_A$ and the single unknown $\alpha_A-\alpha_B$, equivalently the single unknown $\alpha_B$.
Evaluating $g^{-1}$ at $\eta_B(\mathbf{x})$ for any $\mathbf{x}$ is therefore possible once $\alpha_B$ is
pinned, which @thm-mlumr-model does from the comparator outcome summary. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**SPFA versus SEMA.** In the anchored triangle of Chapters 17 and 23, $A$ and $B$ are each contrasted with
a common comparator $C$, and SEMA (@def-sema) sets $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}$, so the
$A$-versus-$B$ effect-modification term $(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})^\top\mathbf{x}$
vanishes even when each active treatment is modified relative to $C$. SPFA imposes the same restriction on
the pair $\{A,B\}$: the contrast @eq-spfa-constant-contrast is constant in $\mathbf{x}$ exactly when
$\boldsymbol\beta_A=\boldsymbol\beta_B$. The difference lies elsewhere. With an anchor, each trial supplies a
within-study contrast in which the study baseline and the prognostic effects cancel, so relative constancy
suffices; without one, $\alpha_A-\alpha_B$ compares the absolute levels of two different studies, so the arm
surfaces themselves must transport (@def-conditional-constancy-absolute, @prp-spfa-vs-sema). SPFA must be
defended from external knowledge: that the covariate-outcome relationship is the same whichever treatment a
patient receives. With a single comparator summary it is untestable, because that summary cannot identify
the comparator slope (@thm-mlumr-identifiability).
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

These results correspond to M.2 in the proof catalogue.

## The SPFA-invoking ML-UMR model {#sec-mlumr-model}

We assemble the model and prove that, under SPFA, it is identified from exactly the available evidence: a
$(d+1)$-dimensional index arm and a one-dimensional comparator outcome summary.

**The identification argument in one breath.** The theorem below is long, but its logic is the four-step
roadmap of @sec-mlumr-roadmap made rigorous. In words: the index IPD estimate one slope
$\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ and one intercept $\alpha_A$ for arm $A$ (an ordinary GLM fit, so both are
identified whenever the covariates are not collinear); SPFA lets that same slope be reused for arm $B$; the
single comparator outcome summary then fixes the one remaining unknown, the comparator intercept
$\alpha_B$, because arm $B$'s average outcome rises monotonically with $\alpha_B$ and so meets the observed
value exactly once. That is the whole argument; the formal statement only names the regularity conditions
that make each step go through. Two symbols recur that the chapter otherwise uses without introduction.
$\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}$ is the *individual-level* outcome distribution, the GLM likelihood kernel for one
patient (a Bernoulli response, say, or a censored survival contribution); $\pi_{\mathrm{Agg}}$ is the
*aggregate-level* distribution of a reported summary (a binomial event count, a normal sample mean). Both
are inherited from Chapters 20 and 25. We write $\theta_{\bullet B}$ for the comparator's *aggregate mean*,
the arm-$B$ average outcome over the comparator covariate distribution, the bullet marking the covariate
that has been averaged out.

::: {#thm-mlumr-model}
## The SPFA ML-UMR model and its identifiability
Adopt SPFA @eq-spfa, so the arm predictors are @eq-spfa-predictors with parameter
$\boldsymbol\xi=(\alpha_A,\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}},\boldsymbol\phi)$, where
$\boldsymbol\phi$ is any dispersion parameter. The model is:

*Individual level (index $A$, IPD).* For $i=1,\dots,n_A$ with covariates $\mathbf{x}_i$,
$$
Y_i^{(A)}\mid\mathbf{x}_i\ \sim\ \pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}\!\big(g^{-1}(\alpha_A+\mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}),\,\boldsymbol\phi\big).
$$ {#eq-mlumr-model-ind}

*Aggregate level (comparator $B$, AgD).* The comparator outcome summary has mean equal to the aggregate
response-scale average over the comparator covariate distribution,
$$
\theta_{\bullet B}=\int_{\mathcal{X}}g^{-1}\!\big(\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\big)\,f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
\qquad
\text{summary}_B\ \sim\ \pi_{\mathrm{Agg}}(\theta_{\bullet B},n_B),
$$ {#eq-mlumr-model-agg}
the aggregate model of @def-aggregate-model specialized to the comparator arm.

Suppose (i) the index design has full column rank, that is the matrix $[\,\mathbf{1}\ \ \mathbf{X}_A\,]$
with rows $(1,\mathbf{x}_i^\top)$ has rank $d+1$, and the link $g$ is strictly monotone and differentiable
with $g^{-1}$ strictly monotone; (ii) the comparator covariate density $f_B$ is known (reported, or
reconstructed by the copula method of @thm-mlumr-qmc-marginalization); and (iii) the observed comparator
outcome mean lies in the open range of $g^{-1}$ (for the logit link this simply says the observed
comparator proportion is strictly between $0$ and $1$; for the identity link it is no restriction at all).
Then $\boldsymbol\xi$ is identified: $(\alpha_A,
\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})$ are identified from the index likelihood @eq-mlumr-model-ind, and
$\alpha_B$ is the unique solution of
$$
\Theta_B(\alpha_B):=\int_{\mathcal{X}}g^{-1}\!\big(\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\big)\,f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}\;=\;\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}},
$$ {#eq-mlumr-alphaB-solve}
where $\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}$ is the observed comparator mean. The target estimand
@eq-mlumr-estimand is then identified in every population $\mathcal{P}^{*}$ for which $f_{*}$ is specified.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Identification of the index parameters.* Restricted to the index source, @eq-mlumr-model-ind is a
generalized linear model with linear predictor $\alpha_A+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ and
strictly monotone link $g$. The mean function $\mathbf{x}\mapsto g^{-1}(\alpha_A+\mathbf{x}^\top
\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})$ determines $(\alpha_A,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})$ uniquely: if two
parameter pairs gave the same mean function then, applying the strictly monotone $g$, the affine functions
$\alpha_A+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ and $\alpha_A'+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}'$
would agree for all $\mathbf{x}$ in the index support, and full column rank of $[\,\mathbf{1}\ \ \mathbf{X}_A\,]$
forces $\alpha_A=\alpha_A'$ and $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}=\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}'$. This is the
standard GLM identifiability already used for the IPD arm in @thm-mlnmr-identifiability-2study. The
dispersion $\boldsymbol\phi$, when present, is identified from the index residual variation in the usual
way.

*Identification of the comparator intercept.* With $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ known from the previous
step and $f_B$ known by hypothesis (ii), the comparator aggregate mean @eq-mlumr-model-agg is the function
$\alpha_B\mapsto\Theta_B(\alpha_B)$ of @eq-mlumr-alphaB-solve. This is exactly the map $\Theta$ of the
aggregate-monotonicity lemma @lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone, with scalar shift $c=\alpha_B$ and
$h(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$. By that lemma $\Theta_B$ is finite,
continuous, and strictly increasing, hence injective, with range the open interval that is the range of
$g^{-1}$; by hypothesis (iii) the observed mean $\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}$ lies in that range, so
the equation $\Theta_B(\alpha_B)=\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}$ has a unique solution. Thus $\alpha_B$
is identified.

*Identification of the estimand.* With $(\alpha_A,\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})$ identified, both
arm predictors @eq-spfa-predictors are determined, so the target arm means $\bar\theta_k(\mathcal{P}^{*})=
\int g^{-1}(\eta_k(\mathbf{x}))f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}$ are determined for any specified $f_{*}$, and
the contrast @eq-mlumr-estimand is their link-scale difference. The integrals are finite under the
integrability hypothesis implicit in (iii) and the boundedness of $g^{-1}$ for the standard links. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This is the payoff of the whole setup, and it is worth stating as a slogan: *one IPD
arm plus SPFA plus one aggregate number is exactly enough to place both treatments in any population.* The
index regression does the heavy lifting (a slope and a level), SPFA supplies the bridge (reuse the slope),
and the comparator's single reported outcome supplies the last degree of freedom (the comparator level).
Nothing is over-determined and nothing is missing; the model is *just identified*. That tight accounting is
also the warning label: with only one comparator number to spend, there is none left over to test SPFA.

::: {#def-mlumr-model-types}
## Type 1 and Type 2 ML-UMR models
Two data regimes recur throughout, and we name them once. The **Type 1 model** invokes SPFA (@def-spfa) and
uses a *single overall* comparator outcome summary; it identifies the comparator intercept $\alpha_B$ only,
reusing the index slope $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$, and is the model of @thm-mlumr-model. The **Type 2
(relaxed) model** drops SPFA, allows a distinct comparator slope $\boldsymbol\beta_B$, and needs *subgroup*
comparator outcomes to identify both $\alpha_B$ and $\boldsymbol\beta_B$ (@thm-spfa-relaxation). Type 1 is
the default, because subgroup outcomes are rarely published; Type 2 is the principled remedy when effect
modification cannot be ruled out and enough subgroups are reported. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

@tbl-mlumr-identifies records which piece of evidence supplies which parameter, and, crucially, whether it
is observed, reconstructed, or merely assumed. The single row marked "assumed" is SPFA, and it is the row
the data cannot audit in Type 1.

| Data source | What it identifies or supplies | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Index IPD (arm $A$) | index level $\alpha_A$ and prognostic slope $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ | observed patient rows |
| SPFA (external belief) | that arm $B$'s slope equals $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ | assumed; untestable in Type 1 |
| Comparator outcome summary (arm $B$) | comparator level $\alpha_B$ | observed aggregate |
| Comparator covariate distribution $f_B$ | the weighting of the arm-$B$ aggregate integral | reported margins, reconstructed via copula |
| Comparator subgroup outcomes | comparator slope $\boldsymbol\beta_B$ as well (Type 2) | rarely observed |
| Target distribution $f_{*}$ | the population the contrast is reported in | chosen from the HTA question |

: What identifies what in ML-UMR. Read top to bottom, this is the four-step roadmap of @sec-mlumr-roadmap
with each step's data source and epistemic status made explicit. Only $\alpha_A$, $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$,
and $\alpha_B$ are estimated from data; $f_B$ is reconstructed; SPFA and $f_{*}$ are supplied from outside
the two studies. {#tbl-mlumr-identifies}

::: {.remark}
**The two families in closed and not-closed form.** For a **continuous** outcome with the identity link and
the linear model $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathbf{x}]=\alpha_k+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$,
aggregation is exact (@thm-identity-link-exact): $\theta_{\bullet B}=\alpha_B+\bar{\mathbf{x}}_B^\top
\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$, so @eq-mlumr-alphaB-solve solves in closed form,
$$
\alpha_B=\bar y_B-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_B^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}},
$$
needing only the comparator covariate *mean*. For a **binary** outcome with the logit link, Bernoulli
individual model and binomial aggregate model, $\Theta_B(\alpha_B)=\int\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B+
\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}$ has no closed form
(@thm-logit-no-closed-form), and @eq-mlumr-alphaB-solve is solved numerically after the integral is
evaluated by the QMC rule of @thm-mlumr-qmc-marginalization; here the comparator covariate *distribution*,
not just its mean, enters. This is the binary "Type 1" model of @chandler2025mlumr; the reference software
`mlumr` fits it as one joint Stan model rather than by the two-step solve, but the two-step solve is what
the identifiability argument exhibits and what the worked example of @sec-mlumr-example carries out by hand.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Bayesian inference.** In practice one does not separate the two steps. Place priors on
$(\alpha_A,\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})$, for example weakly informative normals, and sample the
posterior of the joint likelihood @thm-mlumr-joint-likelihood by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (@def-hmc,
@carpenter2017stan); the QMC integral makes the comparator likelihood a smooth function of the parameters
(@eq-qmc-fixed-nodes), so the gradient HMC needs is available. (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is, for present
purposes, a black-box sampler that draws from the posterior using its gradient; @def-hmc has the mechanics,
and nothing below depends on them.) The reason to fit both blocks jointly, rather than run the two-step
solve of the proof, is *uncertainty propagation*: the joint posterior carries the estimation error in
$\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ from the index arm through into the uncertainty in $\alpha_B$, and hence
into every target-population contrast, whereas plugging a single point estimate of
$\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ into a separate solve for $\alpha_B$ would understate that uncertainty. The
two-step identification argument is the guarantee that the posterior concentrates: the index data pin
$(\alpha_A,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})$
and the comparator mean then pins $\alpha_B$, so the likelihood has a unique maximizer in the limit.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This theorem corresponds to M.3 in the proof catalogue.

## Relaxing SPFA with comparator subgroups {#sec-mlumr-relaxed}

SPFA fails whenever the covariate genuinely modifies the treatment effect, that is when
$\boldsymbol\beta_A\ne\boldsymbol\beta_B$. A single aggregate outcome mean cannot then identify the model,
because it supplies one equation for the $(d+1)$ unknowns $(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)$. The remedy of
@chandler2025mlumr is to demand more aggregate equations, by partitioning the comparator population into
subgroups and using a reported outcome in each. Concretely, this means the comparator report must give, say,
response rates separately for biomarker-positive and biomarker-negative patients, or Kaplan-Meier curves per
risk stratum, each with its own covariate summary. The intuition is a counting argument any reader can hold
onto: each subgroup outcome is one equation, the unknowns are the $d+1$ numbers $(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)$,
and you need at least as many *genuinely different* equations as unknowns. "Genuinely different" is the
catch, and the theorem makes it precise. Such stratified reporting is the exception rather than the rule,
which is why the Type 1 model of @thm-mlumr-model remains the workhorse.

::: {#thm-spfa-relaxation}
## Identifiability of the relaxed model from comparator subgroups
Drop SPFA and allow a treatment-specific comparator slope: the arm predictors are
$\eta_A(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_A+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_A$ and
$\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_B$ with possibly distinct
$\boldsymbol\beta_A,\boldsymbol\beta_B\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$. Suppose the comparator source reports outcomes
for $Z$ non-overlapping subgroups $z=1,\dots,Z$, with known within-subgroup covariate densities $f_B^{z}$
and observed aggregate means $\theta_{\bullet B}^{z,\mathrm{obs}}$, modeled by
$$
\theta_{\bullet B}^{z}(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}g^{-1}\!\big(\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_B\big)\,f_B^{z}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
\qquad z=1,\dots,Z.
$$ {#eq-spfa-relaxed-agg}
Let $\boldsymbol\psi=(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ and write
$w_z(\mathbf{x}):=(g^{-1})'(\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_B)>0$. If

1. (**counting**) $Z\ge d+1$, and

2. (**non-degeneracy**) the $Z\times(d+1)$ matrix $M$ with rows
$\mathbf{m}_z^\top=\int w_z(\mathbf{x})\,(1,\mathbf{x}^\top)\,f_B^{z}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}$ has rank
$d+1$ at $\boldsymbol\psi$,

then $\boldsymbol\psi=(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)$ is locally identified by the $Z$ subgroup equations
@eq-spfa-relaxed-agg, given $\alpha_A,\boldsymbol\beta_A$ from the index IPD. In particular two binary
effect modifiers crossed into $Z=4$ subgroups identify $\boldsymbol\beta_B\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$. If instead
$Z<d+1$, the solution set of @eq-spfa-relaxed-agg is a manifold of dimension at least $d+1-Z\ge 1$, and
$\boldsymbol\psi$ is *not* identified.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Local identification when $Z\ge d+1$ and $M$ has full column rank.* Define the map
$F:\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\to\mathbb{R}^{Z}$ by $F(\boldsymbol\psi)=(\theta_{\bullet B}^{1}(\boldsymbol\psi),\dots,
\theta_{\bullet B}^{Z}(\boldsymbol\psi))$. Each component is differentiable, and by differentiating under
the integral sign (the integrand and its $\boldsymbol\psi$-gradient are bounded for the standard links, so
dominated convergence applies),
$$
\frac{\partial\theta_{\bullet B}^{z}}{\partial\alpha_B}=\int w_z(\mathbf{x})\,f_B^{z}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
\qquad
\frac{\partial\theta_{\bullet B}^{z}}{\partial\boldsymbol\beta_B}=\int w_z(\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{x}\,f_B^{z}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
$$
so the Jacobian $DF(\boldsymbol\psi)$ is exactly the matrix $M$ with rows $\mathbf{m}_z^\top=\int w_z
(1,\mathbf{x}^\top)f_B^{z}$. By hypothesis (2) $M$ has rank $d+1$, its full column rank; since $Z\ge d+1$
by hypothesis (1), $DF(\boldsymbol\psi)$ has a left inverse, and the constant-rank form of the inverse
function theorem gives a neighborhood of $\boldsymbol\psi$ on which $F$ is injective. Hence $\boldsymbol\psi$
is the unique parameter in that neighborhood reproducing the observed subgroup means
$(\theta_{\bullet B}^{z,\mathrm{obs}})_z$: it is locally identified. (The index parameters
$\alpha_A,\boldsymbol\beta_A$ are identified from the IPD as in @thm-mlumr-model, separately from the
comparator block.)

*Non-identification when $Z<d+1$.* The Jacobian $DF(\boldsymbol\psi)=M$ is then a $Z\times(d+1)$ matrix
with $Z<d+1$, so its rank is at most $Z<d+1$ and its kernel has dimension at least $d+1-Z\ge 1$. By the
constant-rank theorem (or directly, by the implicit function theorem applied to the rank-$Z$ system) the
level set $\{\boldsymbol\psi':F(\boldsymbol\psi')=F(\boldsymbol\psi)\}$ contains, near $\boldsymbol\psi$, a
smooth submanifold of dimension $\ge d+1-Z\ge 1$; every point of it reproduces the same $Z$ subgroup means.
Distinct parameter values therefore give identical observable aggregate data, so $\boldsymbol\psi$ is not
identified. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What the subgroups must deliver.** The non-degeneracy condition (2) is the requirement that the $Z$
subgroups differ enough in their covariate distributions: the rows $\mathbf{m}_z$ are the
hazard-weighted subgroup moments of $(1,\mathbf{x})$, and they must span $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$. Two subgroups
with identical covariate means contribute near-parallel rows and add little identifying power, exactly as
two collinear regressors do in least squares. Crossing two binary effect modifiers gives four subgroups
whose means sit at the four corners of a square in covariate space, which generically span $\mathbb{R}^{3}$
and identify $(\alpha_B,\beta_{B,1},\beta_{B,2})$. This is the simulation design of @chandler2025mlumr.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why Type 1 is the default.** Subgroup-specific aggregate outcomes, an event rate or a Kaplan-Meier curve
reported separately within each effect-modifier stratum, are rarely published. When they are not, only the
single overall comparator mean is available, $Z=1<d+1$, and by the theorem the relaxed model is not
identified; one must invoke SPFA and fit the Type 1 model of @thm-mlumr-model. Even when a few subgroups
are reported, the `mlumr` documentation warns that the comparator slope $\boldsymbol\beta_B$ is "weakly
identified by aggregate data," meaning that $M$, while of full rank, is ill-conditioned, so informative
priors or many subgroups are needed for stable estimation. The relaxed model is the principled way to
accommodate effect modification, but its data demands are stringent. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-mlumr-relaxed-subgroups}
## Two subgroups identify a slope, but only if they differ
Take one binary covariate ($d=1$), the logit link, and the index parameters already fixed. The comparator
now reports its response rate in two subgroups. In the favorable case the subgroups are the two covariate
strata themselves: subgroup $z=0$ is the biomarker-negative patients (covariate mean $0$) with observed
response $0.30$, and subgroup $z=1$ is the biomarker-positive patients (covariate mean $1$) with observed
response $0.55$. Each subgroup integral @eq-spfa-relaxed-agg is then a single point, so the two equations
read
$$
\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B)=0.30,\qquad \operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B+\beta_B)=0.55,
$$
which solve exactly: $\alpha_B=\operatorname{logit}(0.30)=-0.85$ and
$\alpha_B+\beta_B=\operatorname{logit}(0.55)=0.20$, so $\beta_B=1.05$. Two aggregate numbers have identified
both the comparator intercept and its slope, with no SPFA invoked. This is the Type 2 model, and the count
$Z=2=d+1$ meets the counting condition with room to spare on non-degeneracy, because the two subgroup means,
$0$ and $1$, are as far apart as they can be.

Now spoil it. Suppose instead the two reported subgroups are "younger" and "older" patients, and the
biomarker prevalence is almost the same in both, say covariate means $0.48$ and $0.52$. Each equation is now
$\theta_{\bullet B}^{z}\approx(1-\bar x_z)\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B)+\bar x_z\operatorname{expit}
(\alpha_B+\beta_B)$ with $\bar x_z$ near $0.5$ in both, so the two equations are nearly the *same* equation:
together they pin the average level well, but say almost nothing about the slope $\beta_B$, because shifting
a little covariate mass between two nearly identical strata barely changes either subgroup's outcome. The
matrix $M$ of @thm-spfa-relaxation is then ill-conditioned; a small error in either reported rate swings the
estimated $\beta_B$ wildly. Counting ($Z=d+1$) is satisfied, yet non-degeneracy nearly fails, and only
strong priors or a genuinely different third subgroup rescue the estimate. This is the arithmetic behind the
`mlumr` warning that the relaxed comparator slope is "weakly identified by aggregate data." $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This theorem corresponds to M.4 in the proof catalogue.

## Aggregate marginalization by quasi-Monte Carlo {#sec-mlumr-qmc}

The aggregate integrals @eq-mlumr-model-agg and @eq-spfa-relaxed-agg are, except on the identity link,
intractable in closed form. ML-UMR evaluates them with the exact pipeline ML-NMR uses, reconstructing the
comparator covariate distribution from its reported margins and a correlation matrix and integrating on the
unit hypercube. The result is a corollary of the hypercube-integration theorem of Chapter 22, recorded here
in the unanchored notation.

**Why an integral, and why the mean is not enough.** Here is the practical reason for the machinery, in one
paragraph. Arm $B$'s average outcome is $\int g^{-1}(\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})
f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}$. On the *identity* link $g^{-1}$ is linear, so the integral equals $g^{-1}$
evaluated at the mean covariate $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_B$: the comparator's reported *means* are all you need. On
the *logit* link (and the hazard scale, and every nonlinear link) $g^{-1}$ is curved, so the average of the
outcome is *not* the outcome at the average covariate; the whole *distribution* of covariates matters, not
just its mean. But the comparator paper reports margins, not patient rows. So the model *fabricates* a cloud
of synthetic covariate points whose margins and correlations match what the paper reported, and averages the
outcome over that cloud. The theorem below is the recipe for building the cloud, an inverse-CDF transform
for each margin glued by a Gaussian copula for the correlations, together with a guarantee that a modest
number of well-chosen points (a Sobol' quasi-Monte Carlo net) makes the average accurate. A reader content
with this picture may skim the theorem and rejoin at the discrete remark, where a single binary covariate
collapses the integral to an exact two-point sum.

::: {#thm-mlumr-qmc-marginalization}
## QMC marginalization of the comparator integral
Let the comparator covariate distribution $f_B$ have marginal distribution functions
$F_{B,1},\dots,F_{B,d}$ (Normal for a continuous covariate of reported mean and standard deviation,
Bernoulli for a binary covariate of reported prevalence, and so on) and Gaussian-copula correlation matrix
$\boldsymbol\Omega_B=LL^\top$ (@def-gaussian-copula). Let $T:[0,1]^{d}\to\mathcal{X}$ be the transport map
of @eq-qmc-pipeline built from these margins and $L$. Then for any integrand $\varphi:\mathcal{X}\to
\mathbb{R}$, in particular the response-scale arm mean $\varphi=g^{-1}\circ\eta_B$,
$$
\int_{\mathcal{X}}\varphi(\mathbf{x})\,f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}=\int_{[0,1]^{d}}\varphi\big(T(\mathbf{u})\big)\,d\mathbf{u},
$$ {#eq-mlumr-qmc-pullback}
and the Sobol' QMC estimate over a net $P_N=\{\mathbf{u}^{(n)}\}_{n=1}^{N}$ (@def-sobol-net),
$$
\widehat\theta_{\bullet B}^{(N)}(\boldsymbol\xi)=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^{N}g^{-1}\!\big(\alpha_B+T(\mathbf{u}^{(n)})^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\big),
$$ {#eq-mlumr-qmc}
satisfies, whenever the pullback $\psi=g^{-1}\circ\eta_B\circ T$ has bounded Hardy-Krause variation
(@def-hardy-krause-variation; intuitively, $\psi$ is not too wiggly on the cube, the multivariate analogue
of a one-dimensional function of bounded total variation),
$$
\big|\widehat\theta_{\bullet B}^{(N)}-\theta_{\bullet B}\big|\le V_{\mathrm{HK}}(\psi)\,D_N^{*}(P_N)=O\!\Big(V_{\mathrm{HK}}(\psi)\,\frac{(\log N)^{d}}{N}\Big).
$$ {#eq-mlumr-qmc-error}
The same pipeline, with $f_B$ replaced by the target density $f_{*}$, evaluates the target arm means
$\bar\theta_k(\mathcal{P}^{*})$ of @eq-mlumr-estimand.
:::

::: {.proof}
The change-of-variables identity @eq-mlumr-qmc-pullback is part 1 of @thm-hypercube-integration: the map
$T$ pushes the uniform law on $[0,1]^{d}$ forward to $f_B$, by the inverse-CDF transform (@thm-inverse-cdf)
on each margin and Sklar's theorem (@thm-sklar) for the Gaussian copula, so the expectation of
$\varphi(\mathbf{X})$ under $\mathbf{X}\sim f_B$ equals the cube integral of $\varphi\circ T$. Substituting
$\varphi=g^{-1}\circ\eta_B$ and the Sobol' net gives @eq-mlumr-qmc. The error bound @eq-mlumr-qmc-error is
the Koksma-Hlawka inequality (@thm-koksma-hlawka) applied to $\psi$ on the cube with the point set $P_N$,
exactly as in part 2 of @thm-hypercube-integration, and the Sobol' discrepancy rate
$D_N^{*}=O((\log N)^{d}/N)$ yields the stated rate. The hypothesis $V_{\mathrm{HK}}(\psi)<\infty$ holds for
$d=1$ with a continuous margin and a bounded monotone link ($\psi$ is then bounded and monotone), but can fail
for $d\ge2$ with normal margins even for the logit link, because $\Phi^{-1}$ has unbounded derivatives at the
faces of the cube (the caveat of Chapter 22); the rate is then not guaranteed by Koksma-Hlawka and the
integration error is checked empirically (@def-integration-error-monitoring).
Replacing $f_B$ by $f_{*}$ changes only the margins and correlation fed into $T$, leaving the argument
verbatim. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Discrete margins and the exact finite sum.** When a covariate is discrete, its inverse distribution
function is a step function, and the pullback $\psi$ is piecewise constant in that coordinate, so its
Hardy-Krause variation can be large and the smooth-integrand rate @eq-mlumr-qmc-error need not hold. This
is not a defect in low dimension: a single binary covariate makes the integral an exact two-point sum,
$\theta_{\bullet B}=(1-\bar x_B)\,g^{-1}(\alpha_B)+\bar x_B\,g^{-1}(\alpha_B+\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})$, with no
QMC error at all, and the worked example of @sec-mlumr-example uses this exact form. For several discrete
covariates, or mixed discrete and continuous sets, one enumerates the discrete cells and applies QMC within
each continuous slice, or uses a randomized (Owen-scrambled; Owen, 1998) Sobol' net whose error behaves
better on non-smooth integrands. The reference software defaults to $N=64$ Sobol' points and provides a
doubling diagnostic, `check_integration()`, the empirical convergence check of @def-integration-error-monitoring,
to verify that the integration error is negligible against the Markov chain Monte Carlo error before the
results are interpreted. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Fixed nodes, smooth likelihood.** As in ML-NMR, the integration nodes $\mathbf{x}^{(n)}=T(\mathbf{u}^{(n)})$
depend only on the comparator's reported margins and correlation, not on the parameters $\boldsymbol\xi$;
they are computed once. The aggregate mean @eq-mlumr-qmc is then a deterministic smooth function of
$\boldsymbol\xi$ with an exact gradient, which is what makes the joint posterior amenable to Hamiltonian
Monte Carlo (@eq-qmc-fixed-nodes). Resampling the nodes at each step, as plain Monte Carlo would, would
make the likelihood noisy and destroy the gradient; this is the same reason QMC, not Monte Carlo, is the
integration rule throughout Part V. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This corresponds to M.5 in the proof catalogue.

## Time-to-event outcomes {#sec-mlumr-tte}

Survival is the outcome that motivates ML-UMR in oncology HTA, where the comparator is a single-arm trial
reporting a Kaplan-Meier curve. The general-likelihood ML-NMR framework of Chapter 25 already extended
aggregation from means to arbitrary individual likelihoods (@thm-general-likelihood-mlnmr); ML-UMR uses
that framework in the unanchored setting, with SPFA acting on the log-hazard scale. We state the model and
its consequences, building directly on the survival results of Chapter 25.

**The survival workflow, before the formalism.** Picture the archetypal case from @exm-mlumr-running: a
single-arm trial of a new agent in advanced melanoma provides IPD (each patient's covariates and survival
time, some censored), while the comparator is a published chemotherapy trial showing only a Kaplan-Meier
curve and a numbers-at-risk table. The analysis is a five-stage pipeline, and it helps to see the whole
pipeline before the theorems dissect it.

1. **Reconstruct** pseudo-individual event and censoring times from the comparator's published Kaplan-Meier
curve and at-risk table (@thm-pseudo-ipd-reconstruction). These pseudo-patients carry times but *no
covariates*.
2. **Attach a covariate cloud.** Pair the reconstructed comparator times with the comparator's reported
covariate distribution $f_B$, the same Gaussian-copula reconstruction used for binary outcomes
(@thm-mlumr-qmc-marginalization); the covariates are integrated out, not matched one-to-one to pseudo-patients.
3. **Integrate the censored likelihood** over that covariate cloud, arm by arm, to form each source's
contribution to one joint likelihood (@eq-mlumr-censored-agg, @thm-mlumr-joint-likelihood).
4. **Fit the posterior** by HMC, borrowing the index prognostic slope for the comparator through SPFA on
the log-hazard scale.
5. **Read off target estimands.** For any chosen population, push the posterior through the covariate
integral to get marginal survival, marginal hazard, RMST, and median survival (@thm-mlumr-target-survival).

A word on direction, because survival flips the sign convention of the binary example. There a *higher*
response probability was better, so a positive $\Delta_{AB}$ favored $A$. With survival a *lower* hazard is
better and a *longer* survival is better: a hazard ratio of $A$ versus $B$ below $1$, or an RMST difference
($A$ minus $B$) above $0$, favors the index treatment. We keep each estimand's numerator explicit and
restate the direction at each use.

::: {#thm-mlumr-tte}
## ML-UMR for time-to-event outcomes
Let the index and comparator hazards follow a parametric survival model with shared baseline shape and
SPFA on the log-hazard scale.

*Proportional hazards (PH).* With a baseline hazard $h_0(t)>0$ and SPFA prognostic slope
$\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$,
$$
h_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})=h_0(t)\,\exp\!\big(\eta_k(\mathbf{x})\big),
\qquad \eta_k(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_k+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}},\quad k\in\{A,B\},
$$ {#eq-mlumr-ph}
which is the PH model @eq-genlik-ph with the single unanchored contrast $\alpha_A-\alpha_B$ in place of the
treatment effect and no effect-modification term.

*Accelerated failure time (AFT).* With an error distribution $F_\epsilon$ and scale $\sigma$,
$\log T=\eta_k(\mathbf{x})+\sigma\epsilon$, $\epsilon\sim F_\epsilon$.

Then:

**(a) Likelihood.** The index contributes the right-censored individual likelihood @eq-genlik-censored-lik
at observed covariates; the comparator contributes, for each (possibly reconstructed) observation
$(t_i,\delta_i)$ with unobserved covariates distributed as $f_B$, the integrated censored likelihood
$$
L_i^{(B)}(\boldsymbol\xi)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}h_B(t_i\mid\mathbf{x})^{\delta_i}\,S_B(t_i\mid\mathbf{x})\,f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
$$ {#eq-mlumr-censored-agg}
well defined and finite by @thm-marginal-individual-likelihood and evaluated by the QMC rule
@thm-mlumr-qmc-marginalization.

**(b) Conditional log hazard ratio.** Under PH and SPFA the conditional log hazard ratio of $A$ versus $B$
is the time-invariant, covariate-free, population-free scalar
$$
\log\frac{h_A(t\mid\mathbf{x})}{h_B(t\mid\mathbf{x})}=\eta_A(\mathbf{x})-\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_A-\alpha_B
\qquad\text{for all }t,\mathbf{x},
$$ {#eq-mlumr-cond-loghr}
by @thm-conditional-loghr-ph and @eq-spfa-constant-contrast.

**(c) Target-population marginal survival, hazard, RMST.** For any target $\mathcal{P}^{*}$, the marginal
survival is the covariate average $S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\int S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,
d\mathbf{x}$; the marginal hazard is the survivor-weighted average @eq-genlik-survivor-rep; and the
restricted mean survival time is the collapsible average $\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=
\int\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}$ of @thm-rmst-collapsible.

**(d) The marginal hazard ratio is time-varying.** Even under the conditional PH and SPFA of @eq-mlumr-ph,
the marginal hazard ratio $h_A(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})/h_B(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})$ is in general not constant
in $t$, and is population-dependent, by @thm-marginal-hr-time-varying.

**(e) Scale misalignment: RMST is collapsible but not freely transportable.** Although the RMST contrast is
collapsible within any population, it is *not* transportable across populations from the log-hazard model.
Precisely, under @eq-mlumr-ph with $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\ne\mathbf{0}$ and $\alpha_A\ne\alpha_B$,
the conditional RMST contrast $\mathbf{x}\mapsto\operatorname{RMST}_A(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})-
\operatorname{RMST}_B(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})$ is a non-constant function of $\mathbf{x}$ whenever
$\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ ranges over an interval, so its population average
$$
\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\big[\operatorname{RMST}_A(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})-\operatorname{RMST}_B(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})\big]\,f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}
$$ {#eq-mlumr-rmst-transport}
depends on the whole distribution of $\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ under $f_{*}$ and in
general differs across target populations, even though the conditional log-hazard contrast
@eq-mlumr-cond-loghr is the single population-free scalar $\alpha_A-\alpha_B$.
:::

::: {.proof}
**(a).** The index term is @def-censored-likelihood, derived from independent censoring in
@prp-censored-likelihood-density. For the comparator, the conditional kernel $h_B(t\mid\mathbf{x})^{\delta}
S_B(t\mid\mathbf{x})$ is a nonnegative function of $\mathbf{x}$ that is a density (in $t$) when $\delta=1$
and a probability (the survival) when $\delta=0$; in either case it is integrable against $f_B$ by
@thm-marginal-individual-likelihood, giving the well-defined @eq-mlumr-censored-agg, and the QMC evaluation
is @thm-mlumr-qmc-marginalization applied to this integrand. (This integrated censored likelihood is the
$\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}=h^{\delta}S$ instance of the general-likelihood theorem @thm-general-likelihood-mlnmr.)

**(b).** By @thm-conditional-loghr-ph the conditional log hazard ratio under PH is $\eta_A(\mathbf{x})-
\eta_B(\mathbf{x})$, free of $t$ and of the baseline; under SPFA this equals $\alpha_A-\alpha_B$ by
@eq-spfa-constant-contrast, free also of $\mathbf{x}$.

**(c).** Marginal survival is by definition the covariate average of conditional survival, and RMST
collapsibility is @thm-rmst-collapsible (a Tonelli exchange of the time and covariate integrals); the
survivor-weighted marginal hazard is @lem-survivor-weighted-hazard. All three carry over verbatim with
$f_{\mathcal{P}}=f_{*}$.

**(d).** Apply @thm-marginal-hr-time-varying: writing $h_B(t\mid\mathbf{x})=h_0(t)e^{\eta_B(\mathbf{x})}$
as a frailty model (one in which each individual's hazard is scaled by a fixed positive multiplier, the
*frailty*) with frailty $\rho(\mathbf{x})=e^{\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}}$
(non-degenerate when $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\ne\mathbf{0}$ and the covariate varies under $f_{*}$),
the constant conditional ratio is $\psi=e^{\alpha_A-\alpha_B}$, and the theorem gives a marginal hazard
ratio that equals $\psi$ only at $t=0$ and is strictly attenuated toward the null for $t>0$, hence
time-varying; the attenuation depends on $f_{*}$ through the survivor distribution
@eq-genlik-survivor-density, hence is population-dependent.

**(e).** Fix two covariate values $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}'$ with $\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}
\ne\mathbf{x}'^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ (possible since $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\ne
\mathbf{0}$). The conditional survival under arm $k$ is, by @thm-survival-hazard-relation,
$S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})=\exp(-e^{\eta_k(\mathbf{x})}H_0(t))$ with $H_0(t)=\int_0^t h_0$, so the conditional
RMST is $\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})=\int_0^{\tau}\exp(-e^{\alpha_k+\mathbf{x}^\top
\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}}H_0(s))\,ds$, a strictly decreasing function of the scalar
$e^{\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}}$ (larger frailty, smaller survival, smaller area). The
contrast
$$
\Delta(\mathbf{x}):=\operatorname{RMST}_A(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})-\operatorname{RMST}_B(\tau\mid\mathbf{x})
=\int_0^{\tau}\Big[e^{-e^{\alpha_A}r(\mathbf{x})H_0(s)}-e^{-e^{\alpha_B}r(\mathbf{x})H_0(s)}\Big]ds,
\quad r(\mathbf{x}):=e^{\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}},
$$
is a function $D(r(\mathbf{x}))$ of $r(\mathbf{x})$ alone. For $r>0$ the integrand of $D(r)$ has the strict
sign of $\alpha_B-\alpha_A$ at every $s\in(0,\tau]$, because $H_0(s)>0$ there ($h_0>0$), so $D(r)\ne0$; and
$D(r)\to0$ as $r\downarrow0$ by dominated convergence. Hence $D$ is not constant on $(0,\infty)$. It extends
to an entire function of $r$ (the integrand is entire in $r$ and bounded on compact sets of $r$ uniformly in
$s\in[0,\tau]$), so by the identity theorem it is not constant on any interval. Therefore
$\Delta(\mathbf{x})$ is non-constant whenever $r(\mathbf{x})$ ranges over an interval, and its average
@eq-mlumr-rmst-transport against $f_{*}$ is a functional of the whole law of $r(\mathbf{X})$, not of a
single moment: two targets whose laws $F_1,F_2$ of $r(\mathbf{X})$ differ give the same
$\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})$ only if $\int D\,d(F_1-F_2)=0$, even though the
conditional log-hazard contrast @eq-mlumr-cond-loghr is the same scalar $\alpha_A-\alpha_B$ in every
population. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Part (e) in two numbers.** The scale-misalignment proof is the densest block in the chapter, so here is a
concrete check with the exponential model of the survival coda (@sec-mlumr-example): $h_k(t\mid x)=
\lambda_k e^{\beta x}$, $\beta=\log 2$, $\lambda_A=0.10$, $\lambda_B=0.15$, horizon $\tau=10$. The
conditional RMST contrast $\Delta(x)=\operatorname{RMST}_A(\tau\mid x)-\operatorname{RMST}_B(\tau\mid x)$
with $\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid x)=(1-e^{-\lambda_k e^{\beta x}\tau})/(\lambda_k e^{\beta x})$ evaluates
to $\Delta(0)=6.321-5.179=1.142$ at $x=0$ and $\Delta(1)=4.323-3.167=1.156$ at $x=1$: *not the same
number*. Because $\Delta(x)$ varies with $x$, its population average shifts with the covariate mix, giving a
target-population RMST contrast of $0.5(1.142)+0.5(1.156)=1.149$ under $P(X=1)=0.5$ but
$0.7(1.142)+0.3(1.156)=1.146$ under $P(X=1)=0.3$. The gap is small in this benign example, but it is
genuine, and not small in general: as $\tau\to\infty$, $\Delta(x)\to(\lambda_A^{-1}-\lambda_B^{-1})e^{-\beta x}$,
which is $3.33$ at $x=0$ and $1.67$ at $x=1$. The conditional log hazard ratio, by contrast, is the single
number $\alpha_A-\alpha_B=\log(\lambda_A/\lambda_B)$ in every population: that is the transportable object, and the RMST contrast is not. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Which estimand to report.** Part (b) gives the clean transportable object: the conditional log hazard
ratio, a single number under SPFA, valid in every population. Part (d) warns that the *marginal* hazard
ratio, the quantity a single Cox fit reports, is time-varying and population-dependent, hence not a
transportable parameter; the `mlumr` default reports the scalar marginal hazard ratio as its value at the
start of follow-up, $t=0$, and exposes the full curve through `predict(type = "loghr")`. Part (e) is the
subtle one, and is the unanchored instance of the scale-misalignment caveat flagged after
@thm-rmst-collapsible in Chapter 25: the RMST contrast is collapsible and clinically interpretable, but
because the model is fitted on the log-hazard scale while RMST lives on the time scale, transporting the
RMST contrast to a population with a different covariate distribution requires that target distribution and
is not licensed by SPFA on the log-hazard scale alone. The practical recommendation, following
@chandler2026survival, is to report the conditional log hazard ratio as the primary transportable summary
and the target-population RMST as a collapsible read-out in each named population. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Baselines and distributions.** The reference implementation supports exponential, Weibull, and Gompertz
PH models and their AFT counterparts (exponential-AFT, Weibull-AFT, log-normal, log-logistic, gamma,
generalized gamma), plus flexible M-spline and piecewise-exponential baselines with a random-walk smoothing
prior, following the `multinma` survival models of @phillippo2025general. The choice of baseline shape is
orthogonal to the SPFA structure: SPFA constrains the covariate slope, the baseline $h_0(t)$ is shared
across arms by the PH assumption, and the unanchored contrast is carried entirely by $\alpha_A-\alpha_B$.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This theorem corresponds to M.6 in the proof catalogue.

## Reconstructing pseudo-individual data from a Kaplan-Meier curve {#sec-mlumr-pseudo}

The comparator likelihood @eq-mlumr-censored-agg is a product over individual observations
$(t_i,\delta_i)$, but a published survival study reports a Kaplan-Meier curve and a numbers-at-risk table,
not individual times. We reconstruct pseudo-individual data that reproduce the published curve, and prove
that the reconstruction is exact in the idealized noiseless case.

Recall the Kaplan-Meier (product-limit) estimator. With distinct observed event times $t_1<t_2<\cdots<t_m$,
$n_j$ patients at risk just before $t_j$, and $d_j$ events at $t_j$, the estimator is
$$
\widehat S(t)=\prod_{j:\,t_j\le t}\Big(1-\frac{d_j}{n_j}\Big),
\qquad \widehat S(t)=1\text{ for }t<t_1 .
$$ {#eq-km-product}
Between consecutive event times the number at risk decreases by the events at $t_j$ and by the patients
censored in $[t_j,t_{j+1})$, say $c_j$ of them: $n_{j+1}=n_j-d_j-c_j$.

::: {#thm-pseudo-ipd-reconstruction}
## Exact reconstruction of pseudo-IPD from a Kaplan-Meier curve
Suppose the published report provides, without digitization error, the step survival curve @eq-km-product
(equivalently the event times $t_1<\cdots<t_m$ and the survival values $\widehat S(t_j)$) together with the
numbers at risk $n_1,\dots,n_m$ at the event times and the initial sample size $n_B=n_1+(\text{any
pre-}t_1\text{ censoring})$. Then:

1. The event counts are uniquely determined by the curve and the risk set,
$$
d_j=n_j\Big(1-\frac{\widehat S(t_j)}{\widehat S(t_{j-1})}\Big),\qquad j=1,\dots,m,\ \ \widehat S(t_0):=1,
$$ {#eq-km-inversion}
and the censoring counts are determined by the risk-set recursion $c_j=n_j-d_j-n_{j+1}$ (with $n_{m+1}$ the
final reported at-risk number).

2. Any pseudo-sample $\{(t_i,\delta_i)\}_{i=1}^{n_B}$ that realizes these per-interval event counts $d_j$
and censoring counts $c_j$ (placing $d_j$ events exactly at $t_j$ and $c_j$ censorings anywhere in
$[t_j,t_{j+1})$) has Kaplan-Meier estimator identical to the published @eq-km-product at every $t$.

3. The reconstruction reproduces the published Kaplan-Meier curve exactly but carries no covariate values,
so it informs only the marginal $(t,\delta)$ law and not any covariate-stratified survival.
:::

::: {.proof}
**(1).** From the product form @eq-km-product, consecutive values satisfy
$\widehat S(t_j)/\widehat S(t_{j-1})=1-d_j/n_j$, because the product for $\widehat S(t_j)$ is the product
for $\widehat S(t_{j-1})$ times the single extra factor $(1-d_j/n_j)$. Solving for $d_j$ gives
@eq-km-inversion; the value is uniquely determined because $n_j>0$ and the ratio
$\widehat S(t_j)/\widehat S(t_{j-1})\in[0,1)$ are both given. With $d_j$ known and the at-risk numbers
$n_j,n_{j+1}$ given, the risk-set conservation $n_{j+1}=n_j-d_j-c_j$ solves uniquely for $c_j=n_j-d_j-
n_{j+1}$. (These are nonnegative integers up to the rounding inherent in reading $\widehat S$; the Guyot
algorithm rounds and redistributes to keep the counts integer and the at-risk numbers matched.)

**(2).** Construct a pseudo-sample with exactly $d_j$ events at time $t_j$ and $c_j$ censorings at
arbitrary times in $[t_j,t_{j+1})$. Its Kaplan-Meier estimator is computed from @eq-km-product using its
own event times and risk sets. At time $t_1$ the pseudo-sample has $n_B$ at risk and $d_1$ events, matching
$n_1,d_1$. Inductively, if the pseudo-sample has $n_j$ at risk just before $t_j$ (matching the published
$n_j$), then it has $d_j$ events at $t_j$ and $c_j$ censorings in $[t_j,t_{j+1})$ by construction, so just
before $t_{j+1}$ it has $n_j-d_j-c_j=n_{j+1}$ at risk, matching the published $n_{j+1}$; the censorings in
the open interval contribute no event factor and only reduce the risk set. Hence at every event time the
pseudo-sample has the same $(n_j,d_j)$ as the published data, so its product-limit estimator equals
@eq-km-product factor by factor, at every $t$. (The placement of censorings within an interval is
irrelevant to the estimator, which only counts how many remain at risk at the next event time, so the
reconstruction is unique as a curve even though the exact censoring times are not.)

**(3).** The pseudo-sample is a list of times and event indicators with no covariates attached, so any
statistic computed from the risk-set counts $(n_j,d_j)$ (the Kaplan-Meier curve, the Nelson-Aalen
cumulative hazard, the Kaplan-Meier RMST) is reproduced exactly; statistics that also use the exact
censoring times, such as a parametric censored likelihood, depend on where the censorings are placed within
each interval; and no covariate-conditional statistic is recoverable. This
is the standard limitation: the reconstruction is faithful at the margin and silent about within-strata
structure. $\square$
:::

::: {#exm-mlumr-km-inversion}
## A three-event Kaplan-Meier inversion by hand
Suppose the comparator report gives $n_B=20$ patients, event times $t_1<t_2<t_3$, at-risk numbers
$n_1=20$, $n_2=14$, $n_3=10$ (and $n_4=8$ after $t_3$), and the published step-curve values
$\widehat S(t_1)=0.800$, $\widehat S(t_2)=0.629$, $\widehat S(t_3)=0.503$. Apply @eq-km-inversion with
$\widehat S(t_0):=1$:
$$
d_1=20\Big(1-\tfrac{0.800}{1}\Big)=4,\quad
d_2=14\Big(1-\tfrac{0.629}{0.800}\Big)\approx3,\quad
d_3=10\Big(1-\tfrac{0.503}{0.629}\Big)\approx2,
$$
(the approximations reflect the three-decimal rounding of $\widehat S$), and the risk-set recursion
$c_j=n_j-d_j-n_{j+1}$ gives the censoring counts
$c_1=20-4-14=2$, $c_2=14-3-10=1$, $c_3=10-2-8=0$. So the published curve and at-risk table pin down exactly
$4$ events then $2$ censorings, $3$ events then $1$ censoring, then $2$ events with $8$ still at risk. Any
pseudo-sample placing events and censorings this way reproduces the curve factor by factor (part 2 of the
theorem). **But note what the pseudo-sample does not have: a covariate for any of these $20$ patients.** The
reconstruction recovers the marginal survival times and nothing about who was biomarker-positive or how old
anyone was. That is why the survival likelihood @eq-mlumr-censored-agg still *integrates* over the reported
covariate distribution $f_B$: the pseudo-times supply the $(t,\delta)$ margin, $f_B$ supplies the covariate
cloud, and the two are combined but never matched patient by patient. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**From idealized inversion to the Guyot algorithm.** @thm-pseudo-ipd-reconstruction is the exact
case in which the at-risk number is known at every event time. In practice the numbers at risk are reported
only at a coarse grid of follow-up times, and the survival values are read off a figure with digitization
error. The algorithm of Guyot and colleagues [@guyot2012] solves the same inversion under these realistic
constraints: it allocates censorings between reported at-risk times so that the implied risk sets match the
table, then applies @eq-km-inversion event by event, iterating to reconcile the curve drops with the
at-risk evolution. The output is pseudo-IPD whose Kaplan-Meier curve matches the published one to within
digitization noise; @chandler2026survival apply it to the comparator arm, and the `mlumr` function
`set_agd_surv()` takes the resulting pseudo-IPD as input. Sensitivity analyses over several independent digitizations quantify the reconstruction
uncertainty, which is the price the unanchored survival comparison pays for having only a published figure.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This theorem corresponds to M.7 in the proof catalogue, and supplies the reconstruction whose existence
Chapter 25 invoked in the remark following @thm-aggregate-marginal-likelihood.

## The joint individual-plus-aggregate likelihood {#sec-mlumr-joint}

The two data sources are combined into one likelihood, and one posterior. The factorization is the
unanchored instance of the aggregate arm likelihood of Chapter 25.

::: {#thm-mlumr-joint-likelihood}
## The joint ML-UMR likelihood
Assume the index observations are conditionally independent given their covariates and $\boldsymbol\xi$,
and the comparator observations are conditionally independent given their (unobserved) covariates and
$\boldsymbol\xi$, with comparator covariates drawn independently from $f_B$. Then the joint likelihood of
the index IPD $\mathbf{Y}^{(A)}$ and the comparator data $\mathbf{Y}^{(B)}$ factorizes as
$$
L_{\mathrm{joint}}(\boldsymbol\xi)=\underbrace{\prod_{i=1}^{n_A}\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}\!\big(y_i^{(A)}\mid g^{-1}(\eta_A(\mathbf{x}_i)),\boldsymbol\phi\big)}_{\text{index IPD, covariates observed}}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{\prod_{i=1}^{n_B}\int_{\mathcal{X}}\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}\!\big(y_i^{(B)}\mid g^{-1}(\eta_B(\mathbf{x})),\boldsymbol\phi\big)\,f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}}_{\text{comparator AgD, covariates integrated}},
$$ {#eq-mlumr-joint-lik}
where for survival the kernel is the censored likelihood $h^{\delta}S$ and the comparator factors use the
reconstructed pseudo-IPD of @thm-pseudo-ipd-reconstruction. With a prior $\pi(\boldsymbol\xi)$ the
posterior is $\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathcal{D})\propto L_{\mathrm{joint}}(\boldsymbol\xi)\,
\pi(\boldsymbol\xi)$, and the two sources are weighted automatically by their information content.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Index factor.* In the index source the covariates $\mathbf{x}_i$ are observed, so each individual
contributes its conditional likelihood $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y_i^{(A)}\mid g^{-1}(\eta_A(\mathbf{x}_i)),
\boldsymbol\phi)$ evaluated at the known covariate; conditional independence makes the index likelihood the
product of these, the first factor of @eq-mlumr-joint-lik.

*Comparator factor.* In the comparator source the covariates are unobserved. By
