@thm-marginal-individual-likelihood, the marginal likelihood of one comparator observation $y_i^{(B)}$,
integrating out its covariate distributed as $f_B$, is $\int_{\mathcal{X}}\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y_i^{(B)}\mid
g^{-1}(\eta_B(\mathbf{x})),\boldsymbol\phi)f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}$; by @thm-aggregate-marginal-likelihood,
conditional independence of the comparator outcomes given covariates together with independent covariate
draws makes the comparator likelihood the product of these marginal contributions, the second factor of
@eq-mlumr-joint-lik. (For a binary outcome each comparator observation is marginally Bernoulli with mean
$\theta_{\bullet B}$, so the reported event count has exactly the binomial law of @def-aggregate-model; a
continuous outcome reported as a sample mean enters through the normal aggregate model of
@def-aggregate-model, a large-sample approximation, because one observation's marginal law is a normal
mixture; for survival no single summary is sufficient and the product runs over the
reconstructed pseudo-IPD.)

*Joint factorization and posterior.* The index and comparator sources are independent given $\boldsymbol\xi$
(different patients in different studies), so their joint likelihood is the product of the two factors,
which is @eq-mlumr-joint-lik. Multiplying by the prior and normalizing gives the posterior. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This single likelihood is what makes ML-UMR a *model* rather than a two-step recipe:
the index IPD and the comparator AgD enter one posterior, so uncertainty flows automatically from each
source into the final contrast, and the same fitted object yields the estimand in every target population.
It is the unanchored counterpart of the ML-NMR likelihood of Chapter 20, with the comparator arm's
covariates integrated out instead of observed. The next remark is a caution against over-reading this: more
comparator data sharpen $\alpha_B$ but never test the borrowed slope.

::: {.remark}
**Automatic information weighting, and what it is not.** The posterior weights each source by its
likelihood curvature: a large index sample sharpens $(\alpha_A,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})$, and a large
comparator sample (more events, more at-risk follow-up) sharpens $\alpha_B$ through the aggregate factor.
This is unlike MAIC and STC, which condition on the index IPD and use the comparator data only for
reweighting or for the comparator-arm value; ML-UMR puts both data types into one likelihood and lets the
posterior balance them. What the weighting is *not* is a substitute for the identifying assumption: the
comparator factor informs only the one scalar $\alpha_B$ (Type 1) or the $(d+1)$-vector $(\alpha_B,
\boldsymbol\beta_B)$ when subgroups are reported (Type 2, @thm-spfa-relaxation); the slope
$\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ that projects the index surface onto the comparator arm comes from the IPD
under SPFA, and no amount of comparator data tests that projection in the Type 1 model. The reference model
also has no random-effects term for between-study heterogeneity: the comparator rows are treated as one
population, a limitation recorded in the `mlumr` documentation. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This theorem corresponds to M.8 in the proof catalogue.

## Marginal survival, hazard, and RMST in target populations {#sec-mlumr-target}

From the joint posterior we read off any target-population estimand by pushing the posterior through the
integration pipeline. We state the construction and its convergence.

::: {#thm-mlumr-target-survival}
## Target-population survival estimands from the posterior
Let $\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathcal{D})$ be the ML-UMR posterior @thm-mlumr-joint-likelihood, and fix a
target population $\mathcal{P}^{*}$ with covariate density $f_{*}$ and a horizon $\tau$. For each arm
$k\in\{A,B\}$ define the functionals
$$
S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*};\boldsymbol\xi)=\!\int S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)f_{*}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x},
\quad
\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*};\boldsymbol\xi)=\!\int_0^{\tau}\! S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*};\boldsymbol\xi)\,dt,
$$ {#eq-mlumr-target-functionals}
and the marginal hazard $h_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*};\boldsymbol\xi)$ by the survivor-weighted formula
@eq-genlik-survivor-rep. Then:

1. Each functional is a continuous (indeed smooth) function of $\boldsymbol\xi$, so its posterior is the
well-defined pushforward of $\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathcal{D})$, summarized by posterior draws.

2. The estimands of the table below are obtained from these functionals; the survival and RMST are
collapsible read-outs (averages of conditional quantities), the median is read off the marginal survival
curve (it is not the average of conditional medians), and the marginal hazard ratio and its log are
non-collapsible and time-varying by @thm-mlumr-tte(d).

| Estimand | Formula |
|---|---|
| Marginal survival | $S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\int S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}$ |
| Marginal hazard | $h_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\dfrac{\int h_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})f_{*}}{\int S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x})f_{*}}$ |
| RMST | $\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\int_0^{\tau}S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})\,dt$ |
| RMST contrast | $\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\operatorname{RMST}_A-\operatorname{RMST}_B$ |
| Marginal log HR at $t$ | $\log\!\big[h_A(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})/h_B(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})\big]$ |
| Median survival | the $t$ solving $S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\tfrac12$ |

3. Computed by QMC over $N$ Sobol' nodes for the inner covariate integral and $S$ posterior draws for the
outer parameter integral, the posterior mean of any of these estimands converges, as $N\to\infty$ and
$S\to\infty$, to the true posterior mean, with QMC error $O((\log N)^{d}/N)$ (@thm-mlumr-qmc-marginalization)
and Monte Carlo error $O(S^{-1/2})$; the QMC rate requires the bounded-variation hypothesis of
@thm-mlumr-qmc-marginalization.
:::

::: {.proof}
**(1).** For fixed $\mathbf{x}$ and $t$, $S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol\xi)=\exp(-e^{\eta_k(\mathbf{x};
\boldsymbol\xi)}H_0(t;\boldsymbol\xi))$ is a smooth function of $\boldsymbol\xi$ (composition of the smooth
exponential with the affine $\eta_k$ and the parametric cumulative baseline $H_0$), bounded in $[0,1]$.
Integrating against the probability measure $f_{*}$ preserves smoothness and boundedness by differentiation
under the integral sign (dominated convergence, the derivative bounded by an integrable envelope), so
$S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*};\boldsymbol\xi)$ is smooth in $\boldsymbol\xi$; integrating over $t\in[0,\tau]$
gives the smooth RMST functional by Tonelli (@thm-fubini-tonelli, @thm-rmst-collapsible). A smooth function
of $\boldsymbol\xi$ has a well-defined pushforward law under the posterior, estimated by applying the
functional to each posterior draw.

**(2).** The marginal survival, RMST, and RMST contrast are averages of conditional quantities, hence
collapsible by @thm-rmst-collapsible, and the median is the solution of $S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})=\tfrac12$; the marginal hazard is the
survivor-weighted average @lem-survivor-weighted-hazard, and its ratio across arms is non-collapsible and
time-varying by @thm-mlumr-tte(d). The table simply records these formulas.

**(3).** For each posterior draw $\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)}$, the inner integral $S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*};
\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})$ is approximated by the QMC average $\frac1N\sum_n S_k(t\mid\mathbf{x}^{(n)};
\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})$ over Sobol' nodes $\mathbf{x}^{(n)}=T(\mathbf{u}^{(n)})$ for $f_{*}$, with error
$O((\log N)^{d}/N)$ by @thm-mlumr-qmc-marginalization when its pullback has bounded Hardy-Krause variation. The
posterior mean is then the average over draws, $\frac1S\sum_s(\cdot)$, with Monte Carlo error $O(S^{-1/2})$
by the central limit theorem for the (stationary) posterior sample, exactly as in Bayesian g-computation
(@def-stc-bayes). The two errors add, and both vanish as $N,S\to\infty$. $\square$
:::

Which of the six estimands should a health researcher actually report? @tbl-mlumr-survival-estimands pairs
each with the clinical question it answers and flags whether it travels across populations. The rule of
thumb, defended in the remark below, is to report the conditional log hazard ratio as the transportable
summary and the RMST (or median) as the clinically interpretable read-out *in each named target
population*, and to treat the marginal hazard ratio with care, because it is neither constant in time nor
portable across populations.

| Estimand | Clinical question it answers | Transportable? |
|---|---|---|
| Marginal survival $S_k(t\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})$ | what fraction of this population is alive at $t$ under arm $k$ | population-specific |
| Median survival | the time by which half this population has had the event | population-specific |
| RMST $\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})$ | average event-free time up to horizon $\tau$, per arm | collapsible, but population-specific |
| RMST contrast | average event-free time gained on $A$ versus $B$ up to $\tau$ | collapsible; differs across populations (@thm-mlumr-tte) |
| Marginal hazard ratio at $t$ | ratio of instantaneous event rates in this population at $t$ | not transportable; time-varying |
| Conditional log HR $\alpha_A-\alpha_B$ | the per-patient log hazard ratio, identical for all under SPFA | the single transportable scalar |

: Which survival estimand to report. Everything except the conditional log hazard ratio is
population-specific and must be recomputed for each target $\mathcal{P}^{*}$; the RMST is at least
collapsible (an average of conditional RMSTs), the median is a read-out of the marginal curve, and the
marginal hazard ratio is neither collapsible nor time-constant. {#tbl-mlumr-survival-estimands}

::: {.remark}
**The whole point of the marginalization.** Parts (1) and (3) are what let ML-UMR report a survival
contrast in a population represented by neither trial: choose any $f_{*}$, push the posterior through
@eq-mlumr-target-functionals, and summarize. The honest cost is part (2) together with @thm-mlumr-tte(e):
the marginal hazard ratio is not a single transportable number, and the RMST contrast, though collapsible,
must be recomputed for each target distribution. The transportable scalar is the conditional log hazard
ratio $\alpha_A-\alpha_B$ of @eq-mlumr-cond-loghr, valid in every population under SPFA. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This theorem corresponds to M.9 in the proof catalogue.

## ML-UMR and unanchored STC {#sec-mlumr-stc}

ML-UMR has a pairwise ancestor. We show that, in the comparator population, the SPFA model reduces exactly
to unanchored STC, and that its extension to other targets is what the multilevel formulation buys, at the
cost of SPFA.

Put plainly, and this is the motivation worth holding before the formalism: we want to know exactly what
ML-UMR buys over the simpler method a health researcher may already know. So we prove the two *agree* where
STC is valid, the comparator population, and pinpoint where they *part company*, every other target. The
agreement is reassuring (ML-UMR is not doing anything exotic at the comparator); the extension to other
populations is the entire value added; and SPFA is the price of that extension. A reader who trusts this
paragraph can read the theorem as its proof.

::: {#thm-mlumr-stc-equivalence}
## Equivalence with unanchored STC at the comparator, extension elsewhere
Adopt SPFA and suppose the comparator AgD provide a sufficient outcome summary (an event count, a sample
mean) so that the comparator likelihood factor of @thm-mlumr-joint-likelihood is the aggregate model with
mean $\theta_{\bullet B}$, and let $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$ be the (limiting) maximizer of the joint
likelihood. Then:

1. **(Calibration identity.)** At $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$ the fitted comparator aggregate mean equals the
observed comparator outcome, $\theta_{\bullet B}(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})=\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}$;
equivalently $\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}_B)=\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}$.

2. **(Equivalence at the comparator population.)** With target $\mathcal{P}^{*}=\mathcal{P}_B$, the ML-UMR
estimand @eq-mlumr-estimand equals the unanchored marginal STC contrast of @thm-stc-consistency(2) with $A$
as the subject (Chapter 19 writes the same contrast as $d_{AB(\mathcal{P}_B)}=-\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}_B)$),
namely
$$
\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}_B)=g\!\big(\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_B)\big)-g\!\big(\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}\big),
\qquad
\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_B)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}g^{-1}\!\big(\eta_A(\mathbf{x})\big)f_B(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x},
$$ {#eq-mlumr-stc-equiv}
the index surface integrated over the comparator covariate distribution, contrasted on the link scale with
the observed comparator outcome. Under the conditions of @thm-marginal-stc-unbiased and the unanchored
condition of @thm-stc-consistency(2), both are consistent for $\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}_B)$.

3. **(Strict extension elsewhere.)** For a target $\mathcal{P}^{*}\ne\mathcal{P}_B$, ML-UMR produces
$\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}^{*})$ by integrating both arms against $f_{*}$ using the fitted $\alpha_B$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$, whereas unanchored STC, lacking a model for arm $B$ beyond the observed
comparator outcome, cannot move arm $B$ off $\mathcal{P}_B$. The extension uses SPFA, whereas
@thm-stc-consistency(2) imposes no assumption on the arm-$B$ slope at all.
:::

::: {.proof}
**(1).** Write the comparator factor as the aggregate model $\pi_{\mathrm{Agg}}(\text{summary}_B\mid
\theta_{\bullet B}(\boldsymbol\xi),n_B)$, a one-parameter exponential-family likelihood in the mean
$\theta_{\bullet B}$ (binomial in the event proportion, normal in the sample mean). Its score in
$\theta_{\bullet B}$ vanishes exactly when the fitted mean equals the observed sufficient statistic, the
standard mean-matching property of the exponential family. For any value of the other parameters,
$\theta_{\bullet B}$ is a continuous, strictly monotone function of $\alpha_B$ whose range contains the
observed value (@lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone), so some $\alpha_B$ attains mean matching and thereby
maximizes the comparator factor; the joint maximizer therefore sets $\theta_{\bullet B}(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})
=\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}$, and its remaining components maximize the index factor alone. By @eq-mlumr-model-agg, $\theta_{\bullet B}=\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}_B)$,
giving the identity.

**(2).** At target $\mathcal{P}_B$ the ML-UMR arm means are $\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_B)=\int g^{-1}(\eta_A)
f_B$ and $\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}_B)=\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}$ by part (1), so the estimand
@eq-mlumr-estimand is $g(\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_B))-g(\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}})$, which is
@eq-mlumr-stc-equiv. Unanchored STC (@thm-stc-consistency(2)) fits the outcome surface on the index IPD,
predicts arm $A$ in the comparator population as $\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}}=\int g^{-1}(\eta_A)f_B=
\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_B)$ (the marginal prediction of @def-stc-marginal with $f_B$ in place of $f_{BC}$),
and contrasts it on the link scale with the comparator's observed outcome $g(\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}})$;
with $A$ as the subject this is exactly @eq-mlumr-stc-equiv. Hence the two coincide. Consistency of the arm-$A$ prediction is @thm-marginal-stc-unbiased under correct specification
and transportability of the index surface to $\mathcal{P}_B$, which is the absolute-constancy condition of
@thm-stc-consistency(2); the observed comparator outcome is consistent for the arm-$B$ mean in
$\mathcal{P}_B$ by design. SPFA is not used at $\mathcal{P}_B$: by part (1) the fitted arm-$B$ mean there is
the observed one whatever slope is assigned to arm $B$. The Bayesian version of @eq-mlumr-stc-equiv is the pushforward of the
posterior through the same functional, the Bayesian g-computation of @def-stc-bayes.

**(3).** For $\mathcal{P}^{*}\ne\mathcal{P}_B$, ML-UMR evaluates $\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}^{*})=\int g^{-1}
(\alpha_B+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}$ with the fitted
$\alpha_B$ and the SPFA slope; this requires the arm-$B$ conditional surface at covariate values typical of
$\mathcal{P}^{*}$, which @lem-spfa-absolute-constancy supplies *only because* SPFA fixes the comparator
slope equal to the index slope. Unanchored STC, having fit no outcome model for treatment $B$ (no
comparator IPD), has no value for arm $B$ away from the observed comparator outcome, so it cannot evaluate
$\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}^{*})$; its estimand is defined only at $\mathcal{P}_B$. Thus ML-UMR strictly
extends the set of admissible targets, and the extension is powered by SPFA, an assumption the
comparator-population estimand does not use. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The honest summary.** @chandler2025mlumr state in their conclusions that ML-UMR "simplifies to unanchored
STC in the comparator population"; part (2) is that statement, proved. The value added by ML-UMR is *not*
at the comparator, where it agrees with the older and assumption-lighter STC, but at other target
populations, where STC is silent. That added scope is bought entirely with SPFA. Whether the extra targets
are worth the stronger, untestable assumption is an application-specific judgment, and the safe default,
when SPFA is doubtful, is to report only the comparator-population contrast, where ML-UMR and unanchored STC
coincide. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This theorem corresponds to M.10 in the proof catalogue.

## SPFA versus SEMA {#sec-mlumr-spfa-sema}

We now prove precisely the sense in which the unanchored assumption is stronger than the anchored one.

::: {#prp-spfa-vs-sema}
## SPFA is SEMA without an anchor
Write each arm slope as $\boldsymbol\beta_k=\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$
(@def-individual-model), with a prognostic part $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ shared by all treatments and
interaction vectors $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$. Then:

1. **(Same slope restriction.)** SPFA ($\boldsymbol\beta_A=\boldsymbol\beta_B$) holds if and only if SEMA
($\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}$) holds, and each holds if and only if the conditional
$A$-versus-$B$ contrast $\eta_A(\mathbf{x})-\eta_B(\mathbf{x})$ is free of $\mathbf{x}$ (with $\mathbf{x}$
ranging over a set whose pairwise differences span $\mathbb{R}^{d}$).

2. **(Anchored: relative constancy suffices.)** In the anchored triangle, study $j\in\{AC,BC\}$ has
predictors $\eta_{jk}(\mathbf{x})=\mu_j+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_k+\mathbf{x}^\top
\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ with $\gamma_C=0$ and $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,C}=\mathbf{0}$. The within-study
contrasts $\eta_{jk}-\eta_{jC}=\gamma_k+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ are free of $\mu_j$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta_1$, so combining them requires only that relative effects transport
(@def-conditional-constancy-relative); under SEMA their difference is $\gamma_A-\gamma_B$, free of
$\mathbf{x}$, even when the common interaction is nonzero.

3. **(Unanchored: absolute constancy is needed.)** In the unanchored network each treatment is observed in
its own study, $\eta_k(\mathbf{x})=\alpha_k+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_k$ with $\alpha_k=\mu_{j(k)}+
\gamma_k$ (@lem-mlumr-single-arm-conflation). Then $\alpha_A-\alpha_B$ equals the treatment contrast
$\gamma_A-\gamma_B$ if and only if $\mu_{j(A)}=\mu_{j(B)}$, and the index surface fitted in
$\mathcal{P}_A$ describes arm $A$ in $\mathcal{P}_B$ or $\mathcal{P}^{*}$ only if that surface transports.
Given SPFA, both requirements together are conditional constancy of absolute effects
(@def-conditional-constancy-absolute).

4. **(Strictness.)** SPFA with absolute constancy implies SEMA with relative constancy, and not conversely:
the unanchored assumption set is strictly stronger, and by (1) the whole gap lies in the constancy, not in
the slope restriction.
:::

::: {.proof}
**(1).** $\boldsymbol\beta_A-\boldsymbol\beta_B=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}$ because
$\boldsymbol\beta_1$ cancels, so SPFA and SEMA are the same equation. The contrast is
$\eta_A(\mathbf{x})-\eta_B(\mathbf{x})=c+\mathbf{x}^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_A-\boldsymbol\beta_B)$ for a
constant $c$, and $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{v}$ is constant on a set whose pairwise differences span
$\mathbb{R}^{d}$ if and only if $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$.

**(2).** Subtracting $\eta_{jC}$ from $\eta_{jk}$ within study $j$ removes $\mu_j+\mathbf{x}^\top
\boldsymbol\beta_1$. The anchored estimand is built from these within-study contrasts, each identified in
its own trial and carried to the target by relative constancy; the absolute level $\mu_j$ never needs to
transport. The difference of the two contrasts is $(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)+\mathbf{x}^\top
(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})$, which SEMA reduces to $\gamma_A-\gamma_B$ whatever the
common value of $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}$.

**(3).** A single-arm study identifies only $\alpha_k$, not $\mu_{j(k)}$ and $\gamma_k$ separately
(@lem-mlumr-single-arm-conflation), and $\alpha_A-\alpha_B=(\mu_{j(A)}-\mu_{j(B)})+(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)$, which
equals $\gamma_A-\gamma_B$ if and only if $\mu_{j(A)}=\mu_{j(B)}$. With a common slope, equal baselines mean
that each arm's conditional mean $g^{-1}(\mu_j+\gamma_k+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_k)$ is the same in
both populations, which is @def-conditional-constancy-absolute; the same condition is what lets the index
surface stand in for arm $A$ outside $\mathcal{P}_A$.

**(4).** By (1) SPFA implies SEMA, and absolute constancy implies relative constancy
(@prp-pat-absolute-implies-relative). For the converse failing, take SEMA, hence SPFA, with study baselines
$\mu_{j(A)}\ne\mu_{j(B)}$ and all other parameters shared: every relative effect is the same in both
populations, so relative constancy holds, while the arm surfaces differ by the baseline shift, so absolute
constancy fails. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**One picture.** SEMA and SPFA say the same thing about slopes: the covariates shape $A$ and $B$ alike, so
their contrast is flat. The designs differ in what else must hold. The anchored design combines
within-study contrasts against a common comparator, so study baselines cancel and only relative effects must
transport (@def-conditional-constancy-relative); the unanchored design compares absolute levels from two
different studies, so the arm surfaces themselves must transport (@def-conditional-constancy-absolute).
@chandler2026transport note that ML-UMR "remains subject to strong limitations inherent to unanchored
comparisons"; this proposition locates that limitation in the absolute constancy. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This proposition corresponds to M.11 in the proof catalogue.

## Identifiability and the limits of unanchored comparison {#sec-mlumr-limits}

We collect the identifiability frontier into one theorem and then survey the limits that no estimator can
overcome.

::: {#thm-mlumr-identifiability}
## Identifiability frontier of ML-UMR
In the unanchored two-treatment network, with the index parameters $(\alpha_A,\boldsymbol\beta_A)$
identified from the IPD, the comparator block has the following identifiability:

1. **SPFA, overall AgD (one aggregate mean).** $(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}})$ identified
($\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ from IPD, $\alpha_B$ from the single mean): the model is just identified
(@thm-mlumr-model).

2. **SPFA, subgroup AgD ($Z\ge2$ means).** Over-identified: $\alpha_B$ solves any one subgroup equation,
and the remaining $Z-1$ equations are testable constraints (a goodness-of-fit check on SPFA).

3. **No SPFA, overall AgD.** $(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ is *not* identified from a
single aggregate mean: the solution set of $\Theta_B(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)=\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}$
is a $d$-dimensional manifold.

4. **No SPFA, subgroup AgD with $Z\ge d+1$.** $(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)$ identified under the
non-degeneracy of @thm-spfa-relaxation.
:::

::: {.proof}
**(1)** is @thm-mlumr-model: $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ from the full-rank IPD design and $\alpha_B$ as
the unique root of the strictly monotone $\Theta_B$ (@lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone), one unknown matched by
one equation.

**(2).** Under SPFA, $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ is known from the IPD and only $\alpha_B$ is free, so
each subgroup equation $\Theta_B^{z}(\alpha_B)=\theta_{\bullet B}^{z,\mathrm{obs}}$ determines $\alpha_B$ by
monotonicity; with $Z\ge2$ subgroups the system is over-determined in the single unknown $\alpha_B$, and
the $Z-1$ residual equations are constraints that hold only if SPFA is correct, hence a test of SPFA. In
practice the test is operationalized as a posterior predictive check: fit the SPFA model, then compare each
observed subgroup outcome against its posterior predictive distribution under the fitted single $\alpha_B$;
a systematic discrepancy (some subgroups over-predicted, others under-predicted, in a pattern aligned with a
covariate) is evidence against SPFA. The parametric counterpart is a likelihood-ratio or score test of the
Type 1 model nested in the relaxed Type 2 model of @thm-spfa-relaxation.

**(3).** With $\boldsymbol\beta_B$ free, the map $(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)\mapsto\Theta_B(\alpha_B,
\boldsymbol\beta_B)$ goes from $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ to $\mathbb{R}$; its gradient $\int(g^{-1})'(\alpha_B+
\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_B)(1,\mathbf{x}^\top)f_B$ is a nonzero row vector (the integrand is positive),
so by the implicit function theorem the level set $\{\Theta_B=\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}\}$ is a
smooth manifold of dimension $(d+1)-1=d\ge1$ near any solution. Every point of it reproduces the same
observed mean, so distinct parameters give identical data: not identified. (This is the $Z=1<d+1$ case of
@thm-spfa-relaxation.)

**(4)** is @thm-spfa-relaxation with $Z\ge d+1$ and the full-rank weighted-moment matrix $M$. $\square$
:::

Three structural limits are shared by every unanchored method, ML-UMR included, and follow from the theory
already developed.

::: {.remark}
**Inherent limits.** First, the identifying assumption is untestable in the overall-AgD case: by
@thm-mlumr-identifiability(3) a single comparator mean cannot distinguish SPFA from any effect-modifying
alternative, so SPFA must be defended externally; it becomes testable only with subgroup AgD
(@thm-mlumr-identifiability(2)). Second, no unanchored method can remove confounding by *unmeasured*
prognostic factors: the projection @eq-spfa-projection transports the index surface in the *measured*
covariates only, and an imbalanced prognostic variable omitted from $\mathbf{x}$ biases the absolute arm
positions exactly as in the necessity direction of @thm-unanchored-paic-consistency. Third, the comparator
covariate distribution $f_B$ is reconstructed from reported margins and an assumed correlation
(@thm-mlumr-qmc-marginalization); misspecifying it biases the aggregate integral and hence $\alpha_B$. For
survival, the Kaplan-Meier reconstruction (@thm-pseudo-ipd-reconstruction) adds digitization noise on top.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Empirical behavior under SPFA violation (simulation evidence, not theorems).** The Chandler-Ishak studies
report simulation results under specific data-generating mechanisms; we record them as evidence, not as
proved statements, and the worked example of @sec-mlumr-example derives the qualitative pattern by hand. For
binary outcomes [@chandler2025mlumr], with about 1000 patients per arm and two correlated binary prognostic
factors, the SPFA model estimating the *comparator-population* log odds ratio shows absolute bias below
about $0.009$ and 95% interval coverage near nominal across no-, weak-, and strong-modification scenarios;
the *index-population* (transported) estimate degrades as modification strengthens, with bias around $-0.06$
(about $-11\%$) under weak modification and around $-0.29$ (about $-67\%$) under strong modification, and
coverage falling accordingly. The relaxed model (@thm-spfa-relaxation) restores small bias and near-nominal
coverage when subgroup AgD are available. For survival outcomes [@chandler2026survival], RMST estimands are
near-unbiased with near-nominal coverage when SPFA holds, degrade modestly under weak modification, and show
substantial bias (often exceeding 25% to 30%) and undercoverage in the index population under strong
modification. The robust pattern, derived analytically in @sec-mlumr-example, is that the comparator-
population estimand is anchored by the observed comparator outcome and so resists SPFA violation, while
non-comparator targets are fragile because the wrong slope is extrapolated to a different covariate
distribution. Different mechanisms can give different profiles; these numbers are illustrative, not
universal. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**When to use ML-UMR.** First, a triage against ML-NMR. If even one study connects the index and comparator
treatments through a common comparator, use the *anchored* machinery: Bucher (Chapter 14), network
meta-analysis (Chapter 15), or connected ML-NMR (Chapters 20 to 25), all of which need only relative
constancy and let the IPD estimate effect modification rather than assume it away. Reach for ML-UMR only when the network is
genuinely disconnected, so that no anchor exists and absolute constancy becomes unavoidable. The one-line rule: prefer
ML-NMR whenever a connecting study exists; use ML-UMR when it does not (see @tbl-mlumr-methods). That
settled, the method is appropriate when individual data exist for the index treatment, only aggregate data
exist for the comparator, no connected (anchored) network is available, SPFA is defensible from clinical
knowledge, and the comparator's covariate summaries are reported. Where SPFA is doubtful, the
defensible report is the comparator-population contrast (where ML-UMR coincides with unanchored STC,
@thm-mlumr-stc-equivalence), interpreted as population-specific rather than transportable, in line with the
NICE guidance of @phillippo2016tsd18. The `mlumr` cautions, no between-study heterogeneity term, weak
identification of the relaxed comparator slope, non-collapsibility of the hazard ratio, and the need to
verify integration convergence, are the practical face of these limits. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This theorem corresponds to M.12 in the proof catalogue.

## A worked unanchored example {#sec-mlumr-example}

We carry a complete binary ML-UMR analysis through by hand, choosing one binary covariate so that every
integral is an exact two-point sum (@thm-mlumr-qmc-marginalization, discrete remark) and every number can
be checked with a calculator. This is the running example of @exm-mlumr-running made numerical. The
covariate $X\in\{0,1\}$ is a binary biomarker (say PD-L1 positivity, with $X=1$ for biomarker-positive); the
outcome is a binary response (a good outcome, so a higher probability is better, and biomarker-positive
patients respond better under the fitted index model); the link is the logit, $g=
\operatorname{logit}$, $g^{-1}=\operatorname{expit}$.

**Inputs.** Fitting the index IPD on treatment $A$ returns the prognostic model
$$
\eta_A(x)=\alpha_A+\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}\,x,\qquad \hat\alpha_A=-0.5,\ \ \hat\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}=1.0,
$$
so the index conditional response probabilities are $p_A(0)=\operatorname{expit}(-0.5)=0.3775$ and
$p_A(1)=\operatorname{expit}(0.5)=0.6225$. The comparator AgD on treatment $B$ report $n_B=200$ patients,
$r_B=77$ responders (crude proportion $\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}=0.385$), and biomarker prevalence
$\bar x_B=P(X=1\mid\mathcal{P}_B)=0.50$. The index population has biomarker prevalence
$\bar x_A=P(X=1\mid\mathcal{P}_A)=0.30$. We use the constants $\operatorname{expit}(-1)=0.2689$,
$\operatorname{expit}(-0.5)=0.3775$, $\operatorname{expit}(0)=0.5$, $\operatorname{expit}(0.5)=0.6225$.

The whole analysis lives in the two rows $x=0$ and $x=1$; @tbl-mlumr-worked collects every conditional
probability the steps below use, including the SPFA-violation column of Step 6. Reading it now makes each
step a lookup rather than a fresh computation.

| Covariate $x$ | weight in $\mathcal{P}_B$ | weight in $\mathcal{P}_A$ | $p_A(x)$ | fitted $p_B(x)$ under SPFA | true $p_B(x)$, slope $2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $x=0$ (biomarker-negative) | $0.5$ | $0.7$ | $0.3775$ | $0.2689$ | $0.1694$ |
| $x=1$ (biomarker-positive) | $0.5$ | $0.3$ | $0.6225$ | $0.5000$ | $0.6011$ |

: Every number in the worked example, by covariate stratum. The fitted and true arm-$B$ columns both average
to the observed comparator response $0.385$ under the comparator weights $(0.5,0.5)$, which is why the
comparator-population contrast is unbiased; they diverge pointwise, so under the index weights $(0.7,0.3)$
they average to different values ($0.3383$ versus $0.2989$), which is the index-population bias of Step 6.
{#tbl-mlumr-worked}

**Step 1: identify $\alpha_B$ (@thm-mlumr-model, @eq-mlumr-alphaB-solve).** Under SPFA the comparator
shares the slope $\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}=1.0$. With the binary covariate the aggregate mean is the exact
two-point sum
$$
\Theta_B(\alpha_B)=(1-\bar x_B)\,\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B)+\bar x_B\,\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B+1)
=0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B)+0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_B+1).
$$
This is strictly increasing in $\alpha_B$ (@lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone), so the equation
$\Theta_B(\alpha_B)=0.385$ has a unique root. Bracketing: $\Theta_B(-1.0)=0.5(0.2689)+0.5(0.5)=0.3845$ and
$\Theta_B(-0.9)=0.5(0.2891)+0.5(0.5250)=0.4070$, so the root lies just above $-1.0$; to the precision of
the reported proportion, $\hat\alpha_B=-1.00$. (The fitted aggregate mean $\Theta_B(-1.00)=0.3845$ matches
the observed $0.385$ to within rounding, the exact-calibration identity of @thm-mlumr-stc-equivalence(1).)

**Step 2: the conditional contrast.** Under SPFA the conditional log odds ratio of $A$ versus $B$ is the
single number, free of $x$ and of population,
$$
\eta_A(x)-\eta_B(x)=\hat\alpha_A-\hat\alpha_B=-0.5-(-1.0)=0.5
\qquad(\text{@eq-spfa-constant-contrast}).
$$

**Step 3: the estimand in the comparator population $\mathcal{P}_B$ ($\bar x_B=0.5$).** The arm means are
exact two-point sums:
$$
\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_B)=0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(-0.5)+0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(0.5)=0.5(0.3775)+0.5(0.6225)=0.5000,
$$
$$
\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}_B)=0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(-1.0)+0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(0)=0.5(0.2689)+0.5(0.5)=0.3845,
$$
the latter equal to the observed comparator proportion, as it must be. The marginal log odds ratio is
$$
\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}_B)=\operatorname{logit}(0.5000)-\operatorname{logit}(0.3845)=0-(-0.4706)=0.4706 .
$$

**Step 4: the estimand in the index population $\mathcal{P}_A$ ($\bar x_A=0.3$).** Now integrate against the
index covariate distribution:
$$
\bar\theta_A(\mathcal{P}_A)=0.7(0.3775)+0.3(0.6225)=0.4510,
\qquad
\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}_A)=0.7(0.2689)+0.3(0.5)=0.3383,
$$
$$
\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}_A)=\operatorname{logit}(0.4510)-\operatorname{logit}(0.3383)=(-0.1966)-(-0.6711)=0.4745 .
$$

**Step 5: read the non-collapsibility.** The conditional log odds ratio is $0.5$ in every population
(Step 2), but the marginal log odds ratio is $0.4706$ in $\mathcal{P}_B$ and $0.4745$ in $\mathcal{P}_A$,
both attenuated toward the null $0$ and differing slightly between populations. This is exactly the
collapsibility dichotomy of @thm-target-population-integral(c): on the non-collapsible logit scale the
marginal estimand depends on the whole target distribution, while the conditional contrast does not. The
attenuation and its population dependence are the @def-non-collapsibility phenomenon, here visible in two
hand-computed numbers.

**Step 6: robustness at the comparator, fragility at the index, under SPFA violation.** Suppose the *true*
comparator model has a steeper slope, $\beta_B^{\mathrm{true}}=2.0\ne\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}=1.0$ (strong effect
modification), with a true intercept calibrated so that the comparator-population proportion is still
$0.385$ at $\bar x_B=0.5$: solving $0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(\alpha)+0.5\,\operatorname{expit}(\alpha+2)=
0.385$ gives $\alpha_B^{\mathrm{true}}=-1.59$. Then:

- *Comparator population.* The true arm-$B$ mean in $\mathcal{P}_B$ is $0.385$ by construction, identical to
the SPFA fit of Step 3; the true arm-$A$ mean is $0.5$ (arm $A$ is correctly specified). So the true
$\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}_B)=0.4706$ equals the SPFA estimate: **no bias at the comparator**, because the
observed comparator outcome anchors the arm-$B$ mean there regardless of the slope.

- *Index population.* The true arm-$B$ mean in $\mathcal{P}_A$ ($\bar x_A=0.3$) is
$0.7\,\operatorname{expit}(-1.59)+0.3\,\operatorname{expit}(0.41)=0.7(0.1694)+0.3(0.6011)=0.2989$, whereas
the SPFA model (slope $1.0$, $\hat\alpha_B=-1.0$) gives $\bar\theta_B(\mathcal{P}_A)=0.3383$ from Step 4.
The true index-population log odds ratio is $\operatorname{logit}(0.4510)-\operatorname{logit}(0.2989)=
(-0.1966)-(-0.8525)=0.6559$, while the SPFA estimate is $0.4745$. The bias is $0.4745-0.6559=-0.1814$, about
$-28\%$: **substantial bias at the index population**, because the wrong slope is extrapolated from the
comparator's covariate distribution (mean $0.5$) to the index's (mean $0.3$).

This is the pattern of the simulation evidence in @sec-mlumr-limits, derived by hand: SPFA-invoking ML-UMR is
robust where it is anchored by data (the comparator population) and fragile where it must extrapolate (any
other target), and the fragility grows with the strength of the violated effect modification and with the
distance between the covariate distributions. When SPFA is doubtful, report only $\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}_B)$.

::: {.remark}
**A survival coda.** The same phenomena appear on the time scale. Take an exponential PH model with one
binary covariate, $h_k(t\mid x)=\lambda_k\,e^{\beta x}$, $\beta=\log2$ (here $X=1$ marks a poor-prognosis
stratum, for example elevated LDH, that doubles the hazard; lower hazard is better, so on this time-to-event
scale $X=1$ is unfavorable, unlike the favorable response biomarker of the binary example),
index rate $\lambda_A=0.10$ and comparator rate $\lambda_B=0.15$, so the conditional hazard ratio of $B$
versus $A$ is the constant $\lambda_B/\lambda_A=1.5$ at every $t$ and $x$ (SPFA on the log-hazard scale,
@eq-mlumr-cond-loghr). In a population with $P(X=1)=0.5$, the marginal survival is
$\bar S_k(t)=0.5\,e^{-\lambda_k t}+0.5\,e^{-2\lambda_k t}$, and the marginal hazard ratio
$\bar h_B(t)/\bar h_A(t)$ equals $1.500$ at $t=0$, dips to $1.438$ at $t=5$ and $1.398$ at $t=10$, then
drifts back to $1.491$ by $t=50$: time-varying, attenuated toward $1$, exactly @thm-mlumr-tte(d) and
@thm-marginal-hr-time-varying. The restricted mean survival times to $\tau=10$ are
$\operatorname{RMST}_A=5.32$ and $\operatorname{RMST}_B=4.17$ (each the exact integral
$0.5\frac{1-e^{-\lambda\tau}}{\lambda}+0.5\frac{1-e^{-2\lambda\tau}}{2\lambda}$), a collapsible difference of
$1.15$ time units favoring the index treatment, the collapsible read-out of @thm-mlumr-target-survival.
Recomputing the RMST difference in a population with $P(X=1)=0.3$ gives a different value, the scale-
misalignment of @thm-mlumr-tte(e): collapsible within each population, but not the same number across them.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-mlumr-notes}

Multilevel unanchored meta-regression is the contribution of @chandler2025mlumr, who introduced the binary
and continuous SPFA and relaxed-SPFA models and the simulation evidence summarized in @sec-mlumr-limits, and
of @chandler2026survival, who extended the method to time-to-event outcomes with parametric and flexible
baselines and the Kaplan-Meier reconstruction of the comparator arm. The method is an extension beyond the
2019 thesis of @phillippo2019thesis: it inherits the multilevel network meta-regression framework of
@phillippo2020mlnmr and its general-likelihood extension of @phillippo2025general (Chapters 20 to 25),
specifically the Sobol' quasi-Monte Carlo integration (@def-sobol-net, @sobol1967) with a
Gaussian copula (@def-gaussian-copula, @thm-sklar, @sklar1959) developed in Chapter 22, and reuses that
machinery in the disconnected setting. The reference implementation is the `mlumr` R package of
Sofi-Mahmudi and Chandler, which fits the SPFA and relaxed models by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in Stan
(@carpenter2017stan), alongside frequentist STC and a naive benchmark, and whose documentation supplies the
practical cautions recorded in @sec-mlumr-limits; it is an adaptation of the GPL-3 `multinma` package of
Phillippo. The transportability framing of population-adjusted indirect comparison that situates the
unanchored estimand, conditional constancy of absolute effects (@def-conditional-constancy-absolute) versus
relative effects (@def-conditional-constancy-relative), is developed by @chandler2026transport and in
Chapter 17; the NICE Technical Support Document guidance is @phillippo2016tsd18.

The structural results of this chapter are new statements of the catalogue items M.1 to M.12, proved in the
book's notation. The single-arm conflation (@lem-mlumr-single-arm-conflation) and the constant-contrast lemma
(@lem-spfa-absolute-constancy) make explicit what the unanchored design must assume; the identifiability theorems (@thm-mlumr-model, @thm-spfa-relaxation,
@thm-mlumr-identifiability) rest on the aggregate-monotonicity lemma @lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone of
Chapter 23 and an inverse-function-theorem argument for the relaxed model; the equivalence with unanchored
STC (@thm-mlumr-stc-equivalence) specializes the marginal STC consistency of Chapter 19
(@thm-marginal-stc-unbiased, @thm-stc-consistency) and the generality theorem of Chapter 23
(@thm-mlnmr-generalizes-nma), and @prp-spfa-vs-sema makes precise the relationship to the shared-effect-modifier
assumption (@def-sema): the same slope restriction, paired with absolute rather than relative constancy. The survival development (@thm-mlumr-tte,
@thm-mlumr-target-survival) builds entirely on the general-likelihood survival results of Chapter 25, the
survival-hazard identity (@thm-survival-hazard-relation), the conditional and marginal hazard ratios
(@thm-conditional-loghr-ph, @thm-marginal-hr-time-varying), the censored likelihood
(@def-censored-likelihood, @prp-censored-likelihood-density), the integrated likelihoods
(@thm-marginal-individual-likelihood, @thm-aggregate-marginal-likelihood), and the collapsible restricted
mean survival time (@thm-rmst-collapsible); the scale-misalignment result @thm-mlumr-tte(e) is the
unanchored counterpart of the caveat flagged after @thm-rmst-collapsible. The Kaplan-Meier reconstruction
(@thm-pseudo-ipd-reconstruction) is the exact-inversion form of the algorithm of Guyot and colleagues
[@guyot2012], whose realistic version handles coarse at-risk tables and digitization error.

There is no machine-checked counterpart for this chapter. The companion Coq development
does not formalize ML-UMR: there is no `ML_UMR.v`, and ML-NMR
itself is unformalized for the reasons given in Chapter 25's notes (the integration and survival content
exceed the development's analysis machinery). The algebraic core closest to formalization is the
contrast-cancellation phenomenon of @prp-spfa-vs-sema, which parallels the anchored cancellation in
`theories/EffectModifiers.v`, and the STC reduction of @thm-mlumr-stc-equivalence, whose comparator-
population identity is the unanchored reading of `theories/STC.v`'s `STC_consistent` and
`methods_agree_when_correct`; but the unanchored setting requires absolute-effect transport rather than
contrast transport, a different algebraic structure that is not currently mechanized. The proofs above are
therefore pen-and-paper and self-contained. This chapter corresponds to results M.1 (the unanchored
setting), M.2 (SPFA), M.3 (the SPFA model and identifiability), M.4 (the relaxed model), M.5 (QMC
marginalization), M.6 (time-to-event), M.7 (pseudo-IPD reconstruction), M.8 (the joint likelihood), M.9
(target-population survival), M.10 (equivalence with unanchored STC), M.11 (SPFA versus SEMA), and M.12
(the identifiability frontier and limits) of the proof catalogue in `proofs/M_ml_umr.md`.

## Exercises {#sec-mlumr-exercises}

Throughout, an exercise marked $\star$ has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first three exercises
are conceptual warm-ups that use the tables of this chapter and need no derivation; the remainder build the
computations and proofs.

::: {#exr-mlumr-data-picture}
**(Warm-up: read the data picture.)** A mock HTA dossier reports an index single-arm trial of drug $A$ with
patient-level age, biomarker status, and response; and for the comparator $B$, only the overall response
rate, the sample size, and the mean age and biomarker prevalence (no subgroup outcomes, no covariate
correlation). Using @tbl-mlumr-identifies, state for each of $\alpha_A$, $\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$,
$\alpha_B$, $\boldsymbol\beta_B$, $f_B$, and $f_{*}$ whether this evidence identifies it, reconstructs it, or
leaves it to assumption, and say whether a Type 1 or a Type 2 model is possible (@def-mlumr-model-types).
What single additional item would the report need to make the relaxed model identifiable?
:::

::: {#exr-mlumr-spfa-belief}
**(Interpretation: why SPFA cannot be tested.)** In one short paragraph, explain to a clinical colleague why
the Type 1 ML-UMR model cannot check SPFA from the two studies (cite @thm-mlumr-identifiability), and why an
anchored comparison needs only relative constancy while an unanchored one needs absolute constancy (cite
@tbl-spfa-sema).
Then give one clinical scenario where SPFA is plausible and one where it is clearly false, and say which
target-population estimate would be most, and which least, trustworthy in the false case (cite Step 6 of
@sec-mlumr-example).
:::

::: {#exr-mlumr-when-method}
**(Interpretation: choose the method.)** For each evidence set, decide whether to use anchored NMA or
ML-NMR, Type 1 ML-UMR, Type 2 relaxed ML-UMR, or only unanchored STC, and justify in one sentence using
@tbl-mlumr-methods: (a) two single-arm trials sharing no comparator, the comparator reporting only an
overall response rate; (b) the same, but the comparator reports response rates in four biomarker-by-age
cells; (c) an index and a comparator trial that each contain a common placebo arm; (d) an unanchored pair in
which SPFA is clinically indefensible and only the comparator population matters for the decision.
:::

::: {#exr-mlumr-conflation}
**The conflation, concretely.** In a single-arm index study with the logit link and no covariates, the
model is $\operatorname{logit}P(Y=1)=\mu+\gamma_A$. Show that the likelihood depends on $(\mu,\gamma_A)$
only through $\alpha=\mu+\gamma_A$, that the maximum likelihood estimate of $\alpha$ is
$\operatorname{logit}(\bar y)$ with $\bar y$ the observed response proportion, and that $\mu$ and
$\gamma_A$ are individually unidentified (@lem-mlumr-single-arm-conflation). Explain in one sentence why an
anchored two-arm study does not have this problem.
:::

::: {#exr-mlumr-identify-alphaB}
**($\star$) Identifying the comparator intercept.** With the logit link, SPFA slope $\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}=0.8$, a
single binary covariate with comparator prevalence $\bar x_B=0.4$, and an observed comparator response
proportion $\theta_{\bullet B}^{\mathrm{obs}}=0.30$, write the two-point aggregation equation
$\Theta_B(\alpha_B)=0.30$ explicitly and solve it for $\alpha_B$ to two decimal places by bracketing and
linear interpolation (@thm-mlumr-model, @lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone). Then compute the comparator-
population marginal response under arm $B$ and verify it equals $0.30$. Using an index fit
$\alpha_A=-0.2$, compute the conditional and the comparator-population marginal log odds ratios of $A$
versus $B$, and comment on the gap.
:::

::: {#exr-mlumr-continuous-closed-form}
**Continuous outcomes need only the mean.** For a continuous outcome with the identity link and the linear
model $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid x]=\alpha_k+\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$, prove that
$\alpha_B=\bar y_B-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_B^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{\mathrm{PF}}$ exactly (using
@thm-identity-link-exact), so that ML-UMR for a continuous outcome under SPFA needs only the comparator
covariate *mean*, not its full distribution. Deduce that for the identity link the target estimand
$\Delta_{AB}(\mathcal{P}^{*})=\alpha_A-\alpha_B$ is the same in every target population, and explain why
this collapsibility fails for the logit link.
:::

::: {#exr-mlumr-relaxed-counting}
**Counting subgroups.** In the relaxed model with $d=2$ continuous covariates, you have $Z=3$ comparator
subgroups. State whether $(\alpha_B,\boldsymbol\beta_B)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is identified, citing the counting
condition of @thm-spfa-relaxation, and describe a configuration of subgroup covariate means for which the
non-degeneracy condition (full rank of the weighted-moment matrix $M$) holds and one for which it fails.
What changes if a fourth subgroup is added?
:::

::: {#exr-mlumr-stc-reduction}
**ML-UMR equals unanchored STC at the comparator.** Using the calibration identity
@thm-mlumr-stc-equivalence(1) and the marginal STC prediction of @def-stc-marginal (with $f_B$ in place of
$f_{BC}$), show by direct substitution that at $\mathcal{P}^{*}=\mathcal{P}_B$ the SPFA ML-UMR estimand and
the unanchored STC contrast of @thm-stc-consistency(2), taken with $A$ as the subject, are the same
expression @eq-mlumr-stc-equiv. Then exhibit, in one or two sentences, why STC
cannot produce the estimand at a target $\mathcal{P}^{*}\ne\mathcal{P}_B$ while ML-UMR can, and name the
assumption that powers the difference.
:::

::: {#exr-mlumr-marginal-hr}
**Time-varying marginal hazard ratio.** In the exponential PH survival coda of @sec-mlumr-example
($h_k(t\mid x)=\lambda_k e^{\beta x}$, $\beta=\log2$, $\lambda_A=0.10$, $\lambda_B=0.15$, $P(X=1)=0.5$),
derive the closed form $\bar h_k(t)=\lambda_k\frac{(1-\pi)+2\pi e^{-\lambda_k t}}{(1-\pi)+\pi e^{-\lambda_k t}}$
with $\pi=0.5$ (using @lem-survivor-weighted-hazard), and confirm by direct computation the marginal hazard
ratios $1.500$ at $t=0$, $1.398$ at $t=10$, and the limit $\lambda_B/\lambda_A$ as $t\to\infty$. Explain in
terms of survivor selection (@thm-marginal-hr-time-varying) why the ratio dips below the conditional value
for intermediate $t$ and returns toward it as $t\to\infty$.
:::

::: {#exr-mlumr-rmst-transport}
**($\star$) Collapsible but not transportable, unanchored.** For the exponential PH model of the survival coda,
write $\operatorname{RMST}_k(\tau\mid x)=\frac{1-\exp(-\lambda_k e^{\beta x}\tau)}{\lambda_k e^{\beta x}}$
and hence the population RMST contrast $\Delta\!\operatorname{RMST}_{AB}(\tau\mid\mathcal{P}^{*})$ as a
two-point average over $P(X=1)=\pi^{*}$. Prove that this contrast is collapsible within each population
(@thm-rmst-collapsible) but differs between two populations with $\pi^{*}=0.5$ and $\pi^{*}=0.3$, and give
the numerical difference at $\tau=10$. Relate your finding to @thm-mlumr-tte(e) and contrast it with the
conditional log hazard ratio of $A$ versus $B$, which is the single number $\log(\lambda_A/\lambda_B)$ in
every population.
:::

::: {#exr-mlumr-spfa-violation}
**Where the bias goes.** Reproduce the SPFA-violation calculation of Step 6 of @sec-mlumr-example with a
*weaker* true comparator slope $\beta_B^{\mathrm{true}}=1.5$ (instead of $2.0$): find the calibrated true
intercept $\alpha_B^{\mathrm{true}}$ from $\Theta_B^{\mathrm{true}}(\alpha)=0.385$ at $\bar x_B=0.5$, then
compute the true and SPFA-estimated index-population ($\bar x_A=0.3$) marginal log odds ratios and the bias.
Confirm that the comparator-population bias is zero and that the index-population bias is smaller in
magnitude than the $-0.18$ of the strong-violation case, illustrating @thm-mlumr-identifiability and the
empirical pattern that bias grows with the strength of the violated modification.
:::

Solutions to the starred exercises @exr-mlumr-identify-alphaB and @exr-mlumr-rmst-transport appear in
Appendix F.
